title: Hawaii Gov Josh Green cruises to Democratic primary win, sets up fall matchup with GOP nominee
summary: Democratic Hawaii Gov. Josh Green's 56% approval rating and $3.5 million war chest left three underfunded challengers with no path in the primary.
story: Video captured the confrontation moments before police arrested congressional candidate Kirill Basin on felony terroristic threatening charges after authorities said he threatened a beachgoer with a knife. (Credit: Maile Stiller-Elliott via Storyful)
Democratic Hawaii Gov. Josh Green defeated three little-known primary challengers seeking to lead the Aloha State.

Green, who was first elected governor in 2022, entered the unusual Saturday primary with a 56% approval rating. His primary win makes him a strong favorite for re-election, as the Cook Political Report rates the race 13 points in favor of the Democratic Party.
Green's opponents were David "Duke" Bourgoin, George "Teva" Lucas-Tadeo, a Democratic socialist, and Lauren Kapoliahiʻiaka Shim.
Bourgoin previously ran against Green for governor in 2022, but he captured only 590 votes compared with Green's 158,161. He also lost two bids for Honolulu mayor, in 2022 and 2024.
HAWAII'S DEMOCRATIC LIEUTENANT GOVERNOR INDICTED IN STATE CORRUPTION INVESTIGATION

Gov. Josh Green speaks onstage during the Clinton Global Initiative 2025 Annual Meeting at New York Hilton Midtown on Sept. 25, 2025, in New York City. (JP Yim/Getty Images for New York Hilton Midtown)

Despite the growing popularity of Democratic Socialists across the country, Lucas-Tadeo failed to win over Hawaii Democrats with public Instagram posts promising publicly run grocery stores and the legalization of marijuana.

Neither Lucas-Tadeo nor Shim had campaign websites, and none of Green's three challengers had raised any money in the race as of June 30, according to Honolulu Civil Beat. Meanwhile, Green had raised approximately $3.5 million, far outpacing Republican Gary Cordery, the race's second-highest fundraiser, who had raised about $313,000, according to Civil Beat.

Hawaii has not had a Republican governor since Linda Lingle left office in 2010. In typical election years, the Democratic primary attracts candidates with strong name recognition. For instance, in 2022, the candidates besides Green included Rep. Kai Kahele, D-Hawaii, and former first lady Vicky Cayetano.

"His policies have been fairly popular, there hasn’t been anything he’s done that’s really created a pushback," John Hart, a communication professor at Hawaiʻi Pacific University, told Civil Beat. "So, why would you throw your hat in the ring on a suicide run when there are other offices that are more achievable?"
BABYLON BEE TOUTS LEGAL WIN OVER HAWAII GOVERNMENT'S 'WAR AGAINST POLITICAL MEMES AND SATIRE' IN FEDERAL COURT
Hawaii Gov. Josh Green delivers remarks as President Joe Biden listens during a visit to an area devastated by wildfires in Lahaina, Hawaii, on Aug. 21, 2023. (Mandel NGAN / AFP via Getty Images)

Meanwhile, Green told Civil Beat that his administration responded effectively to the 2023 Lahaina wildfire, which killed 102 people, and flooding from the March Kona low storms, which caused more than $1 billion in damage.

Governor of Hawaii Josh Green, left center, points to damage as he speaks with FEMA Administrator Deanne Criswell during a tour of wildfire damage on Saturday, Aug. 12, 2023, in Lahaina, Hawaii. (AP Photo/Rick Bowmer)
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

"We were very present, and I think pretty competent and compassionate in our response, and we heard from a lot of people — both politicians and just people — that they appreciated that," Green told Civil Beat.

"It just didn’t create a scenario in which another Democrat thought it made sense to run against us," Green continued. "I didn’t set out to get into fights with people, I really just tried to do this job. So, it didn’t create the usual opening where there was a big divide where people would come after me."
Elaine Mallon is a writer for Fox News Digital and Fox Business covering national politics.

title: Hawaii rep cruises to Dem primary win after challenger arrested for beach brawl
summary: Progressive Rep. Jill Tokuda cruised past three Democratic primary challengers in Hawaii's 2nd Congressional District to face Republican Brenton Awa.
story: Police arrested Democratic congressional candidate Kirill Basin after he threatened individuals during a confrontation on a Maui beach.
Progressive Rep. Jill Tokuda, D-Hawaii, cruised to victory in her primary on Saturday, setting up a showdown with Republican state Sen. Brenton Awa in November.
Tokuda is seeking a third term representing Hawaii's 2nd Congressional District, which includes the entire state outside the island of Oahu, as well as rural and suburban parts of Oahu itself.
The nonpartisan Cook Political Report rates the district D+12. That means it's highly likely that Democrats keep hold of it in this year's midterms.
2026 MIDTERMS STATE OF PLAY: KEY RACES UNFOLD AS STEVENS, EL-SAYED BATTLE IN MICHIGAN

Rep. Jill Tokuda speaks as Army Secretary Dan Driscoll and Army Vice Chief of Staff Gen. Christopher LaNeve appear at a House Armed Services Committee hearing on Capitol Hill on May 15, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)

Tokuda defeated three primary challengers to win the Democratic Party nomination, though none posed a significant threat to her campaign despite a wider intraparty civil war that's toppled several House Democrat incumbents throughout the country.
Her fellow delegation member, Rep. Ed Case, D-Hawaii, faced a significant primary challenge from his left in his own race, though Case is seen as much more moderate than Tokuda.
HAWAII DEMOCRATIC HOUSE CANDIDATE FACES FELONY THREAT CHARGES AFTER BEACH FIGHT CAUGHT ON VIDEO

Rep. Ed Case, D-Hawaii, arrives for the start of the House Appropriations Committee markup of several appropriations bills in the Rayburn House Office Building on July 10, 2024. (Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc. via Getty Images)
Tokuda's race did attract some controversy, however, after one of her long-shot opponents was arrested for a violent altercation that was caught on camera at Keawakapu Beach.
Kirill Basin allegedly threatened a man who asked him to turn down his music, according to Honolulu Civil Beat.
Video shows Kirill Basin swinging a beach chair during an Aug. 1 confrontation at Keawakapu Beach in South Kihei, Hawaii. (Maile Stiller-Elliott via Storyful)
A violent clash ensued after a bystander intervened, and Basin allegedly pulled out a knife.

Tokuda told Hawaii News Now that the video was "disturbing" and said "any individual, whether you're running for office or a public citizen, you need to be held accountable for your actions."

title: Dem establishment strikes back as longtime incumbent fends off progressive challenger
summary: Ed Case survived his toughest primary challenge yet from progressive state Sen. Jarrett Keohokalole, who attacked his SAVE America Act vote and Trump stance.
story: Democratic socialist Melat Kiros pulled off a primary upset against 15-term incumbent Rep. Diana DeGette in Denver, signaling a far-left shift. Tom Del Beccaro weighs in on the Democratic Party's fracture and further shift left.
The Democratic establishment won a key battle in the left's ongoing civil war with its socialist insurgency on Saturday.
Longtime Rep. Ed Case, D-Hawaii, won his primary bid to seek another term in the House of Representatives, defeating progressive state Sen. Jarrett Keohokalole.

Case, who served in Congress from 2002 to 2007 and then won again in 2018, faced his toughest primary challenge yet this year. It comes amid a wider showdown between the Democratic establishment and its far-left flank that's seen multiple House incumbents lose to socialist upstarts.
SOCIALIST VICTORIES SHOW DEMS' DESCENT DOWN 'DEADLY PATH OF COMMUNISM,' JOHNSON WARNS

Rep. Ed Case, D-Hawaii, arrives for the start of the House Appropriations Committee markup of several appropriations bills in the Rayburn House Office Building on Wednesday, July 10, 2024. (Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc. via Getty Images)
Keohokalole, who's been in Hawaii's state legislature since 2014, was the most formidable of a group of primary challengers looking to oust Case this year.
Both raised considerable money on the campaign trail, though the incumbent had more money in his war chest at the outset of the race.
Keohokalole criticized Case for not doing enough to stand up to the Trump administration during the president's second term, including President Donald Trump's federal immigration operations.
The sun sets behind the U.S. Capitol on a hot and humid evening on Aug. 4, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Kevin Carter/Getty Images)
The progressive challenger also attacked Case for being one of four House Democrats to vote for Republicans' initial iteration of the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (SAVE) Act in April 2025.
JOHNSON'S STRATEGY TO BYPASS DEMOCRATS' SAVE ACT BLOCKADE SURVIVES KEY VOTE, HANDING GOP BIG WIN

That version would have imposed a federal voter ID requirement at the polls as well as a proof of citizenship mandate for registering to vote, but would have allowed for a written affidavit absent that proof.

Case told Hawaii News Now that he will "never" be someone who votes in lockstep with his party and said of the issue of noncitizen voting, "This has nothing to do with voter suppression. Now, those are fears and there are legitimate fears, and I accept those concerns."
"It’s a solution in search of a problem. There is no security problem in our election system," Keohokalole told the outlet.
Honolulu, on the south coast of the island of Oahu, is the capital of Hawaii and the gateway to this U.S. island chain in the Pacific. (Patrick Pleul/picture alliance via Getty Images)
Case later joined nearly all other House Democrats in opposing an updated version, the SAVE America Act, which would have vastly expanded the federal government's authority over state voter rolls.
He now goes on to face Republican Adriel Lam in November.

Hawaii's 1st Congressional District, which encompasses part of Oahu, including Honolulu, is rated a safe Democratic seat with a Cook Political Report rating of D+13.

title: Trump's 4th of July fireworks display on National Mall confirmed as largest in history
summary: Trump's Freedom 250 fireworks in Washington, D.C., have been officially confirmed as the largest display in history with 840,537 fireworks on the Fourth of July.
story: Fox News anchor Shannon Bream showcases the widespread celebrations for America's 250th birthday across the country. Events include Washington, D.C.'s record-breaking fireworks extravaganza, President Donald Trump's speeches at national landmarks, a gathering of military veterans including a 103-year-old WWII veteran, and an international naval review in New York Harbor. The segment emphasizes patriotic displays and unity.
Nearly two months after President Donald Trump proclaimed Washington, D.C., would launch the "LARGEST FIREWORKS SHOW IN HISTORY," Guinness World Records confirmed it this week.

"The largest firework display consists of 840,537 fireworks, and was achieved by Freedom 250 and Pyrotecnico, Inc (both USA) at an event organized by Event Strategies Inc in Washington D.C., USA, on 4 July 2026," the organization wrote on its website.

Despite weather delays that involved revelers being evacuated from the National Mall, hundreds of thousands of people still watched the Washington, D.C., fireworks that began just before midnight last month.
TOP HIGHLIGHTS FROM TRUMP'S LATE-NIGHT JULY 4 ADDRESS: ‘NO DREAM IN HISTORY IS BIGGER’

President Donald Trump estimated in his speech that a crowd of 350,000 was cut to 150,000 on the Washington, D.C., National Mall for the record-setting fireworks display over the Washington Monument as part of the Freedom 250 celebration on July 4. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc)
The president also gave an abbreviated speech beforehand as part of the "Salute to America" celebration for the 250th anniversary of the country.
Once it got underway, the show lasted for about 40 minutes.
Interior Secretary Doug Burgum explained in June that the fireworks would be launched from several sites because of its immense scale.
"Normally the fireworks are set off right along here," he told the Washington Reporter of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool.
"This year, because of the size and scale of the thing, there are so many locations where the fireworks are going to be going off, including barges," he explained.
FLASHBACK: AS AMERICAN TURNS 250, HERE'S HOW THE NATION CELEBRATED ITS BIGGEST BIRTHDAYS
President Donald Trump speaks during "Salute to America" Fourth of July celebrations on the National Mall in Washington, D.C., on July 4, before the record-breaking fireworks display. (Getty Images)
The White House launched Freedom 250 as a public-private partnership months ago and the president serves as chair of the initiative.
The previous record holder for largest fireworks display was a megachurch’s 2016 New Year's Eve show, which featured 810,904 fireworks, according to The Washington Post.

"On July 4th, America came together to celebrate our nation’s 250th birthday with the largest fireworks display in history — over 850,000 fireworks lighting up the National Mall and the Potomac River, and miles around in a 40-minute spectacular," Freedom 250 spokesperson Danielle Alvarez shared in a statement with Fox News Digital.
AMERICA 250 ATTENDEES FIRE BACK AT CRITICS OF TRUMP'S JULY 4 SPEECH: 'WHAT WE NEEDED TO HEAR'

A fireworks display lights up the National Mall during the "Salute to America" Independence Day celebration in Washington, D.C., in the early morning hours of July 5. The nation is marking the 250th anniversary of the United States Declaration of Independence. (AFP via Getty Images)

Alvarez added, "This historic display shattered the previous global benchmark and stands as a powerful symbol of unity, resilience, and pride as we begin our nation’s next 250 years. Freedom 250 is honored to have brought this moment to millions of Americans, and we thank everyone who made it possible."

"No other president in history could have accomplished the incredible feat that President Trump did at our Nation’s historic 250th birthday celebration, which included an incredible air show, a record-breaking fireworks display, and an inspiring speech delivered before hundreds of thousands of American patriots," the White House said in a statement, according to the Post.
The White House did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital’s request for comment.
Brie Stimson is a Los Angeles-based entertainment and breaking news writer for Fox News Digital.

title: Trump’s White House ballroom foes face ‘very tough argument’ at Supreme Court, legal experts say
summary: Legal experts say the National Trust for Historic Preservation faces a tough standing hurdle at the Supreme Court over Trump's White House ballroom.
story: Chanley Painter reports on the legal battle surrounding White House ballroom construction after an appeals court blocked the project. Former administration official Stephen Miller argues the facility is a national security necessity.

President Donald Trump could win the legal fight over his planned White House ballroom, say two legal experts who believe the U.S. Supreme Court could end the case without weighing in on the underlying constitutional issue.

In a lengthy social media post Friday, Trump vowed to take the fight over his White House ballroom to the Supreme Court after the D.C. Circuit upheld a lower court order blocking above-ground construction. In a 2-1 decision, the appeals court ruled that the project cannot move forward without Congressional approval.

Trump pointed to the dissent written by Judge Neomi Rao, appointed by Trump in his first term, as grounds for appealing the decision to the Supreme Court. Rao argued that the plaintiffs, the National Trust for Historic Preservation, lack legal standing in the case.

The National Trust for Historic Preservation built its case for legal standing around Alison Hoagland, a member who lives near the White House and regularly visits President’s Park. Hoagland said she visits the area about once a month and argued that the proposed ballroom’s size and design would diminish her enjoyment of the area by overshadowing the White House and weakening its aesthetic.
TRUMP SAYS WHITE HOUSE BALLROOM RULING JEOPARDIZES LIVES OF FUTURE PRESIDENTS, VOWS SUPREME COURT APPEAL

President Donald Trump has overseen ongoing construction of the underground military fortress that is going to be below the $400 million privately funded East Wing ballroom. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)
But according to Rao, the National Trust did not establish the kind of injury necessary to invoke the courts’ authority to block the project.

"The district court elevated the aesthetic displeasure of a single passerby over the government’s security interests in the ballroom and the security risks of leaving an open construction site at the President’s home and office," Rao wrote.

Former Justice Department attorney Abhishek Kambli agreed, telling Fox News Digital the National Trust could face a particularly difficult hurdle on standing at the Supreme Court. He noted that, while Congress created the National Trust, the group still must show that its lawsuit is germane to its interests.

"While they do have ownership of some properties, the President's Park, where the White House East Ballroom is, is not one of them," Kambli said. "And I think that's going to be a very tough argument to sustain, especially with the Supreme Court, that's more likely to agree with Rao than they are the [circuit court] majority, given the makeup of the Supreme Court, and the fact that the Supreme Court is very strict on standing."
OBAMA JUDGE RULES ON EFFORT TO BLOCK AMERICA 250 EVENTS AT WH AND LINCOLN MEMORIAL

President Donald Trump displays a rendering of his proposed $250 million White House ballroom as he meets with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte in the Oval Office of the White House in Washington, D.C., on Oct. 22, 2025. (Alex Wong/Getty Images)

"Normally, aesthetic standing requires that you intend to use it," Kambli said. "So, for instance, if you're planning to be visiting the East Ballroom — and even this is kind of a stretch — that's one thing, but if you're someone on the outside that just passes it by, that's a little tougher."

A similar standing issue surfaced earlier in July when U.S. District Judge Amit Mehta, an Obama-appointed judge, rejected a lawsuit seeking to block the America 250 UFC event at the White House. He ruled that the plaintiffs had not met the standard of aesthetic harm to establish standing.
Hans von Spakovsky, a senior legal fellow at Advancing American Freedom, said he expects Trump to prevail on appeal as well, based on the standing issue.

"Under Supreme Court precedent, you cannot bring a claim, you cannot bring a lawsuit, until and unless you can demonstrate a concrete, actual injury," Spakovsky told Fox News Digital. "The idea that a passerby, who claims she will be aesthetically injured because of what she sees at the White House, has an actual injury is absurd, and obviously, and clearly defies that precedent."
If the Supreme Court takes the case, it could resolve it without deciding whether the administration had the legal authority to build the ballroom in the first place.
TRUMP WARNS JUDGE AGAINST SACRIFICING NATIONAL SECURITY BY BLOCKING WHITE HOUSE BALLROOM, DRONE BASE
President Donald Trump holds design for a proposed White House ballroom while speaking to reporters. (Aaron Schwartz/CNP/Bloomberg)

"The Supreme Court won’t rule on the substantive issue if it can dismiss the case based on a lack of standing by the plaintiffs," von Spakovsky said. "I also don’t know of anyone else who could establish standing to bring a lawsuit. Perhaps Congress could collectively, but the chances of that happening are very slim given the partisan divides in both the House and Senate."

The National Trust argued in its lawsuit that federal law requires Congress to approve new construction on federal property in Washington, D.C., while the administration says existing law already gives the president authority to make alterations and improvements to federal property, including the White House.
Kambli agreed with Rao’s reasoning that the terms "alteration" and "improvement" should be understood in their ordinary real-property sense.

"For instance, if I have an extension to my house, it doesn't become a new house," Kambli said. "It's the same house, but that's an improvement done on the house. Or if I tear down some walls and then just create an open living space in my like between my living room and my kitchen, that's also not a new house at that point.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"It's the same house, but there was an alteration or an improvement done, so if you're using real property terms, then it's pretty clear how the statutory authority would make sense," Kambli continued.
Elaine Mallon is a writer for Fox News Digital and Fox Business covering national politics.

title: Fauci in the congressional wringer: A test for Trump's newly-minted attorney general
summary: The contempt of Congress vote against Anthony Fauci now tests new Attorney General Todd Blanche as Democrats warn of weaponized prosecution.
story: Fox News chief congressional correspondent Chad Pergram reports on a Senate panel’s decision to refer Dr. Anthony Fauci to the Justice Department on ‘Special Report.’
Contempt of Congress.
It sounds bad. And it usually is.
But what does it mean?

Holding someone in contempt of Congress usually stems from them refusing to testify before a House or Senate committee or declining to provide documents and information requested by lawmakers. Especially if someone rejects an inquest by subpoena.
REPORTER'S NOTEBOOK: WHY FAUCI'S 111 FIFTH AMENDMENT PLEAS COULD END UP BEFORE THE COURTS
The Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee voted to hold Dr. Anthony Fauci in contempt of Congress. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)
You refuse to cough up the goods, and Congress may try to hold you in contempt.

And if you’re held in contempt, lawmakers may send a referral to the Justice Department. That’s kind of a parliamentary suggestion box, informing the feds that House members or senators believe you’ve earned prosecution.
The Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee voted recently to hold Dr. Anthony Fauci in contempt of Congress for refusing to answer questions at a hearing.

The panel issued a subpoena to compel Fauci’s compliance. Republican senators say that’s all the more reason why Fauci should testify. They point to his pardon by then-President Joe Biden. That’s why they believe Fauci was obligated to answer their inquiries. Instead, he invoked the Fifth Amendment.
"On the advice of counsel, I respectfully decline to answer based upon my rights under the Fifth Amendment of the Constitution," said Fauci.
Twenty-one words. Uttered an astounding 111 times. That’s a grand total of 2,331 words. Fauci never deviated from the script.
WATCH: GOP SPLIT OVER RAND PAUL’S DOJ STRATEGY IN FAUCI CONTEMPT PUSH
Democrats say it was a Republican ruse.

"The goal was to wait for Dr. Fauci to make any kind of misstatement and then have a weaponized Department of Justice file criminal charges for that new statement that would not have been covered by the pardon," Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., said.
So, the panel took action. It voted 8-5 to hold Fauci in contempt. A party line vote.
"I've never voted to hold somebody in contempt. But if there's one person that should be held in contempt, it is Anthony Fauci," said Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla.
The Fauci conundrum could serve as a significant test for Attorney General Todd Blanche in his new role. (Anadolu via Getty Images)
Sen. Gary Peters, D-Mich., is the ranking Democrat on the Senate Homeland Security Committee.
He warned that the GOP gambit is dangerous.

"Criminal contempt is punitive. It does not compel a witness to answer questions or produce the documents we'd all like to see. What we'll do is create a damaging precedent that future witnesses will use to resist legitimate congressional oversight and weaken this committee's ability to compel testimony."
Senate Homeland Security Committee Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., was unbowed.
"We will hand carry this over to the attorney general. We will hand carry this to the district court here in (the District of) Columbia," Paul said.
Even though, at the time, the DOJ only had an acting attorney general.
FAUCI'S NEWLY RELEASED COVID DIARIES REVEAL BIZARRE FIXATION ON FAME AS PANDEMIC DEATHS MOUNTED
However, Paul was freelancing. He ignored the custom of the entire Senate voting to refer someone to the Justice Department for prosecution.

The Kentucky Republican himself previously sent other, unilateral referrals to the DOJ asking for Fauci’s prosecution. But those efforts never even went through committee. Fox can’t locate any precedent for such an independent maneuver. Especially circumventing the Senate floor.

Republicans control the Senate. It’s unclear whether there would be 51 votes to hold Fauci in contempt. But there is almost no scenario where the Senate could find 60 votes to break a filibuster on a contempt of Congress resolution of this nature.
This is why Democrats argued that Paul is out of line.

"No individual center senator and no committee speaks for the entire Senate as a whole," Peters fumed. "The chairman has also suggested he may attempt to refer this matter to the Department of Justice without approval of the full Senate. That would be even more dangerous and widely unprecedented."
Democrats argued that Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., was out of line. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)
The DOJ says it "seriously reviews all congressional referrals." But Democrats believe the GOP’s disregard for Fauci invoking the Fifth could undermine any prosecution.
"It is almost certainly never going to be approved by a court because it violates basic constitutional rights," Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., said.

In a statement, Fauci’s attorney, David Schertler, accused Paul of trying to "weaponize the Justice Department" against his client. Democrats asserted that before Fauci’s hearing, Republicans cut them out of their inquiry.
"We have been excluded from witness interviews," Peters said.
FAUCI HELD IN CONTEMPT AS COVID CELLPHONE LANDS IN HANDS OF SENATE INVESTIGATORS
But Republicans say Democrats showed no interest in their findings and revelations.
"They have all been uploaded on a website that you were invited to join," Paul said. "You never even asked for the password."
However, the Republican inquiry is just starting. Another Senate panel has now obtained a copy of the Health and Human Services phone Fauci used during the pandemic.
"It's frustrating we haven't gotten these devices until now. But now we have them," Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., said on Fox.
Johnson says decrypting that phone could answer questions Fauci refused to address during the hearing.
Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., noted that "it's frustrating we haven't gotten these devices until now." (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

Two interesting developments emerged since Fauci testified in late July. First, the U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, Jeannine Pirro, dropped her prosecution of former Olympian David Hearn for allegedly vandalizing the Reflecting Pool on the National Mall.
President Donald Trump then upbraided Pirro.

Does this mean that Pirro is doing things by the book? Would that diminish chances for prosecution of Fauci? Or, since Pirro enraged the president, could she redeem herself by prosecuting Fauci? After all, Trump said he wanted Fauci prosecuted.
However, the ultimate decision to prosecute is up to the new attorney general, Todd Blanche. Senators Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, and Susan Collins, R-Maine, vowed to oppose Fauci.

With former Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., out, the GOP couldn’t lose any more votes without tanking the nomination. It boiled down to Sen. Bill Cassidy, R-La., who was undecided. Cassidy announced Friday morning he would vote yea on Blanche.

"I am particularly concerned about episodes of apparent lawfare, DOJ bringing suits against political enemies. Presidents of both parties have been guilty of this. It must stop. It should stop now. A never-ending cycle of prosecuting political enemies undermines the rule of law," Cassidy said.
"I'm not entirely satisfied where where this is."
But Cassidy said he was comfortable enough to confirm Blanche.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Democrats will say any prosecution of Fauci is emblematic of the very weaponization which Cassidy fretted about. And this could be a special test case for the new attorney general.
Chad Pergram currently serves as Chief Congressional Correspondent for FOX News Channel (FNC). He joined the network in September 2007 and is based out of Washington, D.C.

title: Graham replacement hopefuls make final pitches before special election: Iran war, DSA, Flock cams and more
summary: Nine Republican candidates clashed over the Iran war, Flock cameras and the filibuster ahead of South Carolina's Aug. 11 Senate primary vote.
story: 'Fox & Friends' breaks down highlights from the South Carolina GOP Senate debate. Candidate Darline Graham pledges 100% support to Donald Trump's agenda and vows to nuke the filibuster.

Nine Republican candidates vying to permanently fill late Sen. Lindsey Graham's Senate seat spoke directly to voters Saturday at an event in Florence County, South Carolina, where they addressed the war with Iran, the rising tide of socialism in the Democratic Party and potential privacy concerns around Flock cameras.

The event was hosted by Alan Wilson, South Carolina's Republican gubernatorial nominee, who pitched the gathering as a kind of "speed dating," since each candidate was given six minutes to address the crowd.
The special Republican Senate primary is scheduled for Aug. 11, which made Saturday's event one of the last chances for the candidates to make their closing arguments to voters.
Here's what they chose to focus on in their elevator pitches.
REPUBLICANS DEFY TRUMP, JUMP INTO SOUTH CAROLINA SENATE RACE DESPITE HIS HANDPICKED SUCCESSOR
Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C., hugs sister Darline Graham on stage as he announces his presidential campaign June 1, 2015. (Jessica McGowan/Getty Images)
Darline Graham
Sen. Darline Graham, chosen to finish out her brother's term after his death in July, was the last to speak but was quick to tell attendees she intended to earn their votes.

"I'm not a politician. I never wanted to be a politician. But like Lindsey, I have a servant's heart. I am a hard worker. And, yes, I have President Trump's endorsement, but I know I have to earn your votes," she said at the beginning of her speech.
She emphasized that she was not a "DEI" candidate, hyping her experience running the South Carolina Commission for the Blind, a state agency with a $90 million budget and dozens of employees.
"We help blind people and people with disabilities get jobs so that they don't have to rely on the government. How is that DEI?" she said.
Sen. Darline Graham, R-S.C., makes her way to votes in the U.S. Capitol Wednesday, Aug. 5, 2026. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)
TRUMP MAY HAVE ENDORSED DARLINE GRAHAM, BUT GOP SENATE HOPEFULS AREN’T BACKING DOWN

She also made sure to highlight issues she and President Donald Trump agree on, including keeping transgender athletes out of female sports, standing with Israel, supporting voter ID through the SAVE Act and ending blanket birthright citizenship.
Graham briefly touched on socialism within the Democratic Party, calling it a problem that has to be stopped. She also described Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., as crazy.
Her speech concluded by answering a question about Flock cameras, which can automatically read license plates and are being installed all over the country.

"I need to look into that one because there's two sides to that story. I know that some people are concerned about privacy and protecting their privacy, and I'm all for protecting the privacy of U.S. citizens. The other side of it is, if there's an emergency situation that an ambulance can be called quicker and it can save lives," Graham said.
"I'm going to be honest. That's a hard one for me. So, I want to look into it a little bit more."
A Flock safety camera is shown mounted to a light pole Aug. 3, 2026 in Beverly Hills, Calif. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)
Ralph Norman
Rep. Ralph Norman, R-S.C., focused on his frustration with the Senate, calling it the place where "good bills go to die."
He proposed overhauling the Senate's rules to get measures like the SAVE Act passed.

"I will use my, whatever expertise I have, to go to the Senate and force the vote, whether it's blowing up the filibuster or having a walking filibuster or getting with the parliamentarian and changing some of these stupid, arcane rules that the Senate has," Norman said.

The Senate filibuster allows a minority of senators to delay or block most legislation, effectively requiring 60 votes to advance a bill and making it harder for a narrow majority to enact its agenda.
Rep. Ralph Norman, R-S.C., speaks to reporters as he leaves a House Republican Conference meeting at the Cannon House Office Building May 20, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)
TRUMP'S VOTER ID BILL CATCHES UNLIKELY BREAK AS MCCONNELL REMAINS SIDELINED
After his remarks, Norman was asked about the extent to which AI data centers should be regulated.
He said the federal government should not have a role but appeared to disagree with Trump's recent full-throated support of bringing data centers to communities around the country.
"Do I think it's bad for the community? Yes. Do I think it hurts the environment? Yes. And I will do whatever I can," Norman said.
An Amazon Web Services data center in Aldie, Va., May 31, 2026. (Lexi Critchett/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Mark McBride
The key takeaway from former Myrtle Beach Mayor Mark McBride's speech is that he broke away from Trump's position on the war with Iran.
"Y'all, there is something we have to address if we're going to win in November," McBride said. "We need to end the war. We need to end the war now.
"We just have to admit we've lost the war. We've lost this battle," he continued. "Come home and regroup for another day."
He then addressed the crowd, saying, "There's not one of y'all in here who voted for President Trump a year and a half ago because this is where you thought we would be."
RETIRED LT. COL. RUNNING FOR CONGRESS BACKS TRUMP IRAN STRATEGY: 'HE'S ENDING A 47-YEAR CONFLICT'
Sam Shepherd
Sam Shepherd, an engineer, inventor and entrepreneur, took the opposite approach to McBride, claiming he is "more conservative than Trump."
Shepherd cast himself as someone who has the skills to fix complex issues within the bureaucracy and the military.
He also took a moment to one-up Elon Musk, the former head of the Department of Government Efficiency, arguing he had more patents than the Tesla billionaire.
"I've actually authored more patents than Elon Musk. I have 44. I'm asking for you to bring common sense back to the government," Shepherd said.
Russell Fry
Rep. Russell Fry, R-S.C., spent much of his speech tying the affordability issues Americans are facing to "onerous regulations."

"We see this on farms. We see this in every manner of our government. Regulations strangle us," he said. "You've got to get government out of the way if we're going to solve this affordability crisis."
In response to a question about how he would secure the border if elected, Fry started off by attacking former President Joe Biden's work ethic and praising Trump's.

"You actually have to have a president who's awake for more than four hours a day, right? We went from a president who slept for 20 and was awake for four, to a president who is awake for 20 and sleeps for four," Fry said.
Fry said he would work to close "loopholes Biden used" to grant thousands of Haitians and Nicaraguans asylum in the U.S.
Rep. Russell Fry, R-S.C., speaks during a GOP stump event held for Republican candidates for Senate in Charleston, S.C., Aug. 6, 2026. (Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)
Mark Sanford
Former South Carolina Gov. Mark Sanford zeroed in on the ballooning national debt, which is about to reach a staggering $40 trillion.
Sanford, who also twice served as a South Carolina congressman, said the debt is incomprehensible and unsustainable.
"We've got a federal government that goes out and spends money it doesn't have, and then it turns around, and it prints money that's not there," Sanford said.
He argued that the growing national debt is inextricably linked to Americans reaching financial and life milestones later in life.

"The average age to buy a house, not that long ago, was 39 years of age, just 15 years ago. Today, that number is 59. In 15 years, it slid back 20 years, which is to say the American dream is becoming that much more difficult whether it's my four boys or y'all's kids or grandkids out there," Sanford said.

Former Gov. and Rep. Mark Sanford, R-S.C., speaks during the GOP stump event held for Republican candidates for Senate in Charleston, S.C., Aug. 6, 2026. (Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)
Mark Lynch
Mark Lynch, a businessman, was another candidate who favored getting rid of the filibuster.
He also said he wouldn’t "take a penny from AIPAC," making him one of the few candidates, along with McBride, to stake out a position at odds with the field’s staunch support for Israel.

Lynch's "No. 1" issue was his strong opposition to abortion. He talked at length about how he has spent time convincing women not to go through with terminating their pregnancies and how he has lobbied state legislators to toughen abortion restrictions.
Mark Lynch speaks during the GOP stump event held for Republican candidates for Senate in Charleston, S.C., Aug. 6, 2026. (Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)
Danny Ford II
Danny Ford II, the son of the championship-winning former head football coach at Clemson University, was the first to address Flock cameras and the potential privacy issues they raise.
He also talked about rapid data center development getting "out of control."
"It's getting pushed straight down our citizens' throats without any say so," he said.
On the issue of data centers, Ford said they need to be sustainable, produce their own power and not "leave a stain on South Carolina."
Glenda Gail Parker

Glenda Gail Parker, a retired budget analyst with the U.S. Air Force, described herself as a conservative independent who leans Republican, but she broke with Trump on energy policy, saying the country needs to reduce its reliance on fossil fuels.

In response to a question about how she would ensure South Carolina farmers get the assistance they need after natural disasters, Parker said she would work to mitigate "the climate extremes that we are experiencing now."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"And I do that by reducing our consumption of fossil fuels and lower[ing] the demand for fossil fuels. In fact, today I want to challenge the oil and gas companies," Parker said. "Those companies that are interested in longevity must realize that they are in the energy business, not the oil and gas business. And so I would like to challenge the oil and gas businesses to clean up their image."
She concluded by saying the U.S. needs to pursue solar, wind, geothermal energy and hydropower.
James Cirrone is a writer on the Breaking/Trending News team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to james.cirrone@fox.com.

title: The Hitchhiker’s Guide to what the Senate did and didn’t do overnight
summary: Despite confirming Todd Blanche as attorney general, the Senate wrapped its summer session with major legislative priorities unresolved.
story: Fox News' chief congressional correspondent Chad Pergram reports on the Senate's race to clear a packed agenda before the recess, including President Donald Trump's demand for a vote on the 'Save America Act' amid legislative hurdles.
The Senate wrapped up its summer session at 4:57 a.m. ET.
Senators knocked two major items off their checklist. They confirmed Todd Blanche as the nation’s 88th attorney general.
They also approved a bipartisan interim spending bill that likely goes a long way toward preventing a government shutdown in October.
But nearly as important as what senators accomplished is what didn’t get done.
REPORTER'S NOTEBOOK: SUMMER ENDS, BUT THE SENATE'S FALL CRUNCH BEGINS
The U.S. Capitol  (Emma Woodhead/Fox News Digital)
The Senate did not stay in session and attempt to pass the SAVE America Act.
In fact, there was not even procedural stunting by the pro-SAVE America Act Republicans, who advocated blowing up the August recess.
TRUMP PUMPS BRAKES ON SENATE BUDGET PLAN, DELAYING GOP SAVE AMERICA PUSH

Moreover, the Senate did not take a vote on a budget framework that could enable them to eventually tack on some election integrity measures and pass them at a later date in a bill not subject to a filibuster.
Expect some conservatives to rail against the Senate for not working this out.
Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio., speaks at the U.S. Capitol. The Senate blocked his voter ID measure in a test vote ahead of the August recess. (Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
The SAVE America Act continues to lack votes. However, advocates of the bill can use the decision by the Senate to leave town without passing it as an opportunity to apply pressure on its opponents.
That said, the Senate did take a test vote on a more narrow voter ID bill backed by Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio. The Senate blocked that bill.

But the test vote got Democrats on the record for opposing it. And giving Husted a vote on his measure was a tactical move to boost his chances in a competitive race this fall against former Sen. Sherrod Brown, D-Ohio.
The Senate did not take a test vote on the bipartisan bill to regulate money for intercollegiate athletics despite the endorsement by the Big 10 and SEC.
PROTECT COLLEGE SPORTS ACT STALLS IN OVERNIGHT SENATE SHOWDOWN, VOTE PUSHED TO SEPTEMBER AFTER CHAOTIC EVENING

In fact, President Trump even implored the Senate to stay in session in August to pass the bill authored by Senate Commerce Committee Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., the top Democrat on the panel.
Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, said the Protect College Sports Act will be "one of our first orders of business" in September. (Heather Diehl/Getty Images)
The legislation was beset by an internecine fight among Republicans about whether the legislation kept men from competing in women’s sports.
The president published a full-throated endorsement of the legislation Friday night, declaring that the measure did go far enough.
"Anyone who tells you otherwise is lying," the President wrote on Truth Social.
In an overnight statement, Cruz said the bill was still in play.
"The good news is that when the Senate returns in September, the Protect College Sports Act will be one of our first orders of business having locked in a vote," Cruz said.
However, no vote is officially secured on the Senate docket.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
But what about a test vote on a bill to regulate cryptocurrency?
It was thought that the Senate might pursue that bill in the closing days of the summer session. But the differences were just too wide to close.
However, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., teed up a procedural vote on cryptocurrency for Sept. 15.
Chad Pergram currently serves as Chief Congressional Correspondent for FOX News Channel (FNC). He joined the network in September 2007 and is based out of Washington, D.C.

title: Joe Biden's cancer has spread further, leaving him in 'very painful' condition, Hunter reveals
summary: Hunter Biden told the BBC his father's prostate cancer has metastasized into his bones, calling it "very painful" and "very debilitating."
story: Former first lady Jill Biden said her husband, former President Joe Biden, would not have been able to serve another four years as president, citing his cancer diagnosis.
Former President Joe Biden's prostate cancer has spread and is causing him significant pain, his son Hunter Biden revealed during a Friday interview.
"The cancer has spread, metastasized into his bones and further," Hunter Biden told the BBC in an interview that aired Friday. "It’s very painful, and it’s very debilitating in many respects.
"It’s really sad to watch," Hunter Biden said. "The only thing that I’d say about my dad, about his health right now, is I wish he would complain more, because it’s not good."
Despite his poor health, Hunter Biden said his father is "still doing his thing," attending speaking engagements.
HUNTER BIDEN CLAIMS UNDER OATH THAT HIS FAMILY IS BROKE AMID FIGHT OVER $17M LEGAL BILL

President Joe Biden, left, and son Hunter Biden, during the Easter Egg Roll on the South Lawn of the White House in Washington, D.C., April 1, 2024. The former president was previously diagnosed with Stage 4 cancer. (Michael Reynolds/EPA/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Joe Biden revealed his prostate cancer diagnosis in May 2025, just months after he departed the Oval Office.
The diagnosis at the time was that the cancer was Stage 4, "aggressive" and had already spread to his bones.
He received a Gleason score of 9, indicating both the cancer's aggressive nature and the potential that he had been living with it for years.
WATCH: WOULD-BE SECOND-TERM PRESIDENT BIDEN LEFT SEARCHING FOR FAMILY ON STAGE AFTER OBAMA CENTER OPENING

"He had it while he was president," said Dr. Ezekiel J. Emanuel, vice provost and oncologist at the University of Pennsylvania, adding Joe Biden "probably had it at the start of his presidency in 2021.
"He did not develop it in the last 100 to 200 days," Emanuel said, according to the American Journal of Medical Care.

Former President Joe Biden speaks to a crowd during a fundraising event with the South Carolina Democratic Party at the Columbia Museum of Art Feb. 27, 2026, in Columbia, S.C. (Sean Rayford/Getty Images)
Joe Biden's wife, Jill, previously told the hosts of ABC's "The View" that his cancer has slowed him down.

"He keeps his schedule, but he’s slowed down," she said in June. "I mean, Stage 4 cancer is — and he's 83 — so, I think the mix of everything and the medications that he's taken has made life a little more difficult these days."

Former first lady Jill Biden was a guest on "The View" June 2, 2026. She told hosts that medications former President Joe Biden has taken have "made life a little more difficult these days." (ABC via Getty Images)
Fox News Digital contacted the Office of Joe and Jill Biden for further comment.

Fox News Digital's Brie Stimson contributed to this report.

title: Hawaii voters hit the polls as Gov Josh Green dominates, progressive takes aim at Dem congressman
summary: Hawaii's 1st Congressional District primary pits Rep. Ed Case against Jarrett Keohokalole, who opposes Donald Trump's tariffs and ICE enforcement.
story: Fox News chief congressional correspondent Chad Pergram reports on Ohio Rep. Max Miller's decision to press ahead with his re-election campaign despite mounting calls for him to resign or withdraw following allegations of abuse.

Hawaii voters cast their ballots on Saturday to decide who advances to the November general election, with key contests including the race for governor and the battle to represent the state’s 1st Congressional District.
Gov. Josh Green, who was first elected in 2022, is heavily favored to win the Democratic primary, where he faces three little-known competitors.
His challengers include George "Teva" Lucas-Tadeo, a Democratic socialist who has promised on social media to open a government-run grocery store and legalize recreational marijuana.

David "Duke" Bourgoin is mounting his second primary challenge against Green after losing to him in 2022, when he captured only 590 votes against Green’s 158,161. He also lost bids for Honolulu mayor in 2022 and 2024.
JOHNSON'S STRATEGY TO BYPASS DEMOCRATS' SAVE ACT BLOCKADE SURVIVES KEY VOTE, HANDING GOP BIG WIN
Democratic Hawaii Gov. Josh Green and GOP candidates Gary Cordeery and Rep. Ed Case, D-Hawaii (Patrick T. Fallon/AFP via Getty Images; Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)
Lauren Kapoliahiʻlaka Shim is also seeking the Democratic nomination. She is the CEO and founder of Aloha AI Incorporated, according to her LinkedIn profile.
Neither Lucas-Tadeo nor Shim had campaign websites, and none of Green’s three challengers had raised any money in the race as of June 30, according to Honolulu Civil Beat.
Green has raised about $3.5 million, far outpacing Republican Gary Cordery, the race’s second-highest fundraiser, who has raised about $313,000, according to Honolulu Civil Beat.

Cordery, owner of the contracting company Kingdom Builders, and Ken Fujiyama, an entrepreneur and investor, are competing for the Republican nomination and a chance to end nearly two decades of Democratic control of the governor’s mansion. The last Republican to serve as Hawaii's governor was Linda Lingle, who held the office from 2002 to 2010.

Hawaii Gov. Josh Green, center, delivers remarks and President Joe Biden listens during a visit to an area devastated by wildfires in Lahaina, Hawaii, Aug. 21, 2023. (Mandel Ngan/AFP via Getty Images)

Cordery has campaigned on lowering Hawaii’s high cost of living, expanding housing and cracking down on government waste and corruption. He has proposed adding 15,000 homes for working families, using state-owned land for housing and eliminating the state’s general excise tax on food and medicine. Fujiyama has also proposed a plan to tackle the housing affordability crisis by developing 100,000 residential lots and partnering with large landowners to spur growth.
MICHIGAN’S TOP ELECTION OFFICIAL WINS DEMOCRATIC PRIMARY FOR GOVERNOR, ADVANCES TO BATTLEGROUND RACE

Whoever emerges from the Republican primary will face an uphill battle to unseat Green if he secures the Democratic nomination. Green holds a 56% approval rating, while the Cook Political Report rates the race "Likely Democrat" and gives Democrats a 13-point advantage.
Eyes outside Hawaii will be locked on the Democratic primary in the 1st Congressional District, where state Sen. Jarrett Keohokalole is challenging Rep. Ed Case, D-Hawaii.

Rep. Ed Case, D-Hawaii, arrives for a House Appropriations Committee markup of several appropriations bills in the Rayburn House Office Building in Washington July 10, 2024. (Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER
Case, who is seeking a seventh term, has represented the district since 2019 and argues that his seniority and position on the Appropriations Committee give Hawaii greater influence in Washington.

Keohokalole, who is endorsed by Our Revolution, a group founded by Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., is running on a progressive platform that includes Medicare-for-all and opposition to ICE and President Donald Trump's tariffs.

Keohokalole is seeking to portray Case as out of touch with Democratic voters, pointing to the congressman’s vote with House Republicans to pass Trump's SAVE America Act, which would require voters to show proof of citizenship when registering to vote.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Given the district’s strong Democratic lean, whoever wins the party’s primary will likely be favored to win the seat in November.
Elaine Mallon is a writer for Fox News Digital and Fox Business covering national politics.

title: 'DEI queen': Virginia Dem's past embrace of far-left prosecutors unearthed
summary: Shannon Taylor's record as Henrico County prosecutor clashes with her tough-on-crime campaign image as she seeks to represent Virginia's 1st Congressional District.
story: Fox News congressional correspondent Bill Melugin reports House Republicans confronting Fairfax County prosecutor Steve Descano over his sanctuary policies on 'Special Report.'

Shannon Taylor, the Democratic nominee in the race for Virginia’s 1st Congressional District, once endorsed progressive prosecutorial blueprints, advocating for less incarceration and more diversity as a Henrico County commonwealth attorney, some of the same "Democratic values" that ended in tragedy in other parts of Virginia.
Shortly after entering the role in 2012, Taylor fired seven prosecutors.
"I stated publicly that the office needs to have more diversity, and I’m going to keep to that public statement," Taylor said in an interview ahead of the firings.

Her track record is sparking criticism that she used her role to prioritize ideological and political views at the expense of public safety. It’s also clashing with portrayals from her campaign, highlighting her work as a tough-on-crime figure as she looks to win over a Republican-leaning district.
FORMER PROSECUTOR WHO ACCUSED TRUMP OF WEAPONIZING DOJ WINS DEM PRIMARY
Shannon Taylor, attorney for Henrico County, exits the Albemarle County Circuit Court in Charlottesville, Va., June 4, 2024. (AP Photo/Ryan M. Kelly, File)
Taylor highlighted her work as she topped a crowded field of Democratic candidates vying to challenge Republican incumbent Rep. Rob Wittman, R-Va.

"As Henrico’s top prosecutor for the last 14 years, Shannon has tried thousands of cases and put violent criminals, drug traffickers and abusers behind bars," Taylor states on her campaign website. "She has a record of shutting down fraudsters trying to take advantage of working families and locking up violent criminals who threaten our safety."
But that hasn’t always been the appearance she’s given.

After her seven firings, Taylor faced blowback for trying to hire a woman named Misty Whitehead as a police oversight prosecutor. However, before the role could be made official, social media posts from Whitehead surfaced that seemingly showed a pattern of attacking police.
Taylor faced backlash from the town’s county manager over her selected candidate.

"A county manager can’t tell a commonwealth’s attorney who to hire, but he can recommend whether or not local funds are included to supplement that salary. And in this case, I absolutely will not do it under any circumstances," County Manager John Vithoulkas said at the time.
Whitehead had a history of voicing concerns about police behavior and social justice that raised concerns for at least one county official, according to local reports.
Taylor defended her pick, telling local outlets that she believed the posts were "thoughtful analysis of the current events we are all living through."
Taylor also has ties to similarly minded prosecutors in other counties, some of whom entered the public eye recently due to tragic circumstances.
SPANBERGER'S ICE ROLLBACK TO BLAME FOR TODDLER's KILLING, VIRGINIA 'HOTBED' OF ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT CRIME: DHS
Abdul Jalloh, 32, right, is accused of killing Stephanie Minter, 41, left, at a bus stop in Virginia. (Fox 5 DC)

In Fairfax County, Virginia, news broke that Abdul Jalloh, a 32-year-old illegal alien from Sierra Leone, stabbed a Virginia resident to death at a bus stop despite over 30 prior arrests and a known tendency for violent behavior.
Jalloh’s criminal record included charges of rape, malicious wounding, assault, drug possession, identity theft, trespassing, larceny and firing a weapon.
Even so, prosecutor Steve Descano had dropped many of them, prompting concern and outrage from lawmakers.
"You dismissed the case, and it’s shameful," Rep. Brad Knott, R-N.C. said at a hearing where Descano was summoned to Congress to explain a series of similar cases.
Knott had been highlighting one such instance involving a child predator.
"When you dismiss a case, what happens to that defendant? He walks free. A disgusting, perverted individual preying on children that you dismissed," Knott said.
Long before Descano’s time in the spotlight, Taylor had endorsed Descano, supporting his bid to become county prosecutor in 2019, citing shared outlooks.

"I am excited to endorse Steve Descano for Fairfax County’s Commonwealth’s Attorney because I know he will prioritize the same Democratic values we all share, making Fairfax a safe and just place for everyone and I am looking forward to working with him," Taylor wrote.
Taylor and Descano went on to champion their shared values in a 2021 letter to the Biden administration.

In it, the two joined 100 other district and county attorneys in championing a set of "21 principles for the 21st-Century prosecutor." The authors claimed that "tough on crime policies" had been "anathema to justice." They championed an end to mandatory minimums and three-strike laws, advocated for taking immigration status into consideration when negotiating sentences and plea deals and opposed calling rapists "rapists," drug dealers "drug dealers" and convicted criminals "felons" or "inmates."
"A number of elected reform-minded prosecutors are boldly redefining what it means to be a prosecutor," the letter states.
OKLAHOMA TEEN ACCUSED OF RAPING TWO GIRLS WALKS FREE; DA FURIOUSLY CALLS IN FEDS: ‘MADE MY BLOOD BOIL’
Fairfax County Commonwealth's Attorney Steve Descano, left, and Fairfax County Sheriff Stacey Ann Kincaid, right, testify before Congress. (Tom Williams/Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
At least one Republican onlooker blasted Taylor’s record.

"She spent her time reshaping the prosecutor's office around identity politics, pushing a far-left agenda that put woke activism ahead of public safety and fighting to turn Virginia into a far-left hellscape," Emma Hall, a spokesperson for the Republican National Committee, said in a statement to Fox News Digital.
"Instead of prosecuting criminals and making Virginia safer, DEI queen Shannon Taylor chose to be a diversity, equity and inclusion consultant."

title: Is cyberbullying hiding in your child's group chat?
summary: Cyberbullying often hides inside jokes, group chats and AI deepfakes. These 15 tips help parents and grandparents start the conversation early.
story: Child and adolescent family therapist Darby Fox explains how teens view social media. New research indicates that while some find platforms like Snapchat beneficial for friendships, most encounter online harassment or bullying on TikTok, Instagram, and other platforms. Fox advises parents to implement strict monitoring and maintain open dialogue to protect their children's mental well-being.

"It was only a joke." Those five words can stop an important conversation before it begins. Maybe your child or grandchild posted a rude comment in a group chat. Another kid added an embarrassing picture. Soon, classmates were sharing it and piling on with laughing reactions.

To the children taking part, it may feel like ordinary online drama. To the child being targeted, every notification can feel like another person joining the attack. The warning signs of cyberbullying are not always obvious. Some children hide what they are experiencing. Others take part without realizing their behavior has crossed a line.

That is why cybersecurity education needs to go beyond strong passwords, antivirus software and password managers. Those protections remain essential. However, children also need guidance about empathy, privacy and the consequences of what they post. Parents play a central role. Grandparents can also become trusted listeners, especially when a child feels nervous about telling Mom or Dad. Share this article with the adults in your family. Then use it to start a conversation before a child needs help.

JEWISH STUDENT TARGETED WITH ANTISEMITIC ABUSE, LAPTOP CORD ATTACK AT COLORADO SCHOOL, ADL ALLEGES
Cyberbullying can spread through group chats, social media and gaming platforms, leaving children vulnerable to rumors, humiliating images and online harassment. (iStock)
Cyberbullying can hide inside ordinary online behavior

Cyberbullying rarely arrives with a warning label. It may appear as a cruel joke, an altered photo or a rumor inside a private chat. Someone might create a fake account to embarrass a classmate. A group may deliberately exclude one child and then share screenshots of the conversation.

The CDC defines bullying as unwanted aggressive behavior that involves a real or perceived power imbalance. The behavior repeats or has a strong chance of being repeated. Cyberbullying occurs when children use texting, social media or other technology to carry out that behavior. That definition can become confusing online.

One person may post something only once. However, dozens of other people can save and share it. The child who created the post may call it a single joke, while the person being targeted watches it circulate for days. Children may also believe they are only watching. Yet forwarding a humiliating image or adding a laughing reaction can make the attack feel much larger. Adults need to help children connect an online action with the real person receiving it.
What the latest cyberbullying data tells families

The latest available research shows that online harassment remains part of daily life for many young people. The CDC reports that more than one in six U.S. high school students experienced electronic bullying during the previous year. That includes bullying through texting and social media. Female students reported it more often than male students.

A World Health Organization study involving 44 countries and regions found that 15% of adolescents had experienced cyberbullying. Meanwhile, 12% admitted cyberbullying someone else. Both figures had increased compared with the organization's earlier research. A 2026 Pew Research Center study offers a closer look at the social platforms teenagers use. Roughly three-quarters of teen TikTok, Instagram and Snapchat users said harassment and bullying were problems on those platforms for people their age.

Nearly three in 10 teen Snapchat users said they had personally experienced at least one form of harassment covered by the survey. Those behaviors included offensive name-calling, rumor spreading or physical threats. The figure was about one in five among teen Instagram and TikTok users. These numbers do not mean every disagreement counts as bullying. Still, families should not wait for an online situation to become severe before discussing it.
Your child may not realize they joined the bullying
Ask a child whether they have bullied anyone and the answer will probably be no. Ask whether they have forwarded an embarrassing screenshot and you may hear a different response.

Children often picture a bully as one openly cruel person who targets someone weaker. Online harassment can look far less organized. A teenager may add an emoji without thinking. Someone else may share the post because everyone at school has already seen it. Another child may remain silent because speaking up could make them the next target.

Each action can increase the pressure on the person being humiliated. Parents and grandparents should avoid starting this conversation with an accusation. Instead, use an example your child can understand.

Ask how the person in the picture might feel. Find out whether they gave permission for the post. You could also ask what your child would want a friend to do if someone shared the same content about them. These questions help children examine their decisions without immediately feeling attacked.
Why telling a child to go offline may not solve it

I recently spoke with a high school senior and her mother, who works in education. The student explained that bullying often looks very different from the scenes adults remember from movies. Much of it happens in private chats, anonymous apps and social media accounts that hide the person posting.

Rumors can spread across a school before the person being discussed knows they exist. AI tools can also produce altered photos, fake audio and convincing videos of a classmate. When I asked whether leaving social media could provide some relief, the student explained that her phone connected her with friends and much of her school life. That response stayed with me.

Adults often see putting down a phone as a break. A teenager may see it as disappearing from their social circle. Leaving an app can also mean missing plans or school updates while everyone else continues discussing the situation.

Pew Research Center found that 74% of teens said social media helped them feel connected to what was happening in their friends' lives. At the same time, 39% said social media made them feel overwhelmed by drama. Nearly one-third said it sometimes left them feeling excluded. "Delete the app" should not be the only advice a child hears.
Parents may feel ready to talk before children feel ready to answer

Adults often assume their children know they can come to them. Children may feel differently. A 2025 Pew Research Center survey found that 80% of parents felt highly comfortable discussing their teenager's mental health. Only 52% of teens felt equally comfortable having that conversation with a parent. That gap should get every parent's attention.

A parent may believe the door is wide open. Meanwhile, the child may worry about losing a phone or being blamed for what happened. The child may also fear that an adult will immediately call the school and make the situation more public.

Grandparents can sometimes help bridge that distance. A teenager may reveal something during a car ride or while visiting for the weekend. The conversation may begin casually instead of during a serious family meeting. Listen closely when a child suddenly asks what you would do in a "hypothetical" situation. They may be testing whether it feels safe to tell you more.
COULD THE 7-ELEVEN BREACH AFFECT YOU?
Children may contribute to cyberbullying without realizing it by forwarding embarrassing screenshots, sharing harmful posts or reacting to humiliating content. (iStock)
AI deepfakes are raising the stakes for children

Generative AI has made a painful form of online abuse much easier to create. A classmate can take an ordinary social media photo and use an AI tool to create a fake nude image. Someone can also clone a voice, produce a false video or build a convincing impersonation account. The National Center for Missing & Exploited Children received more than 400,000 CyberTipline reports with a generative AI connection during 2025.

NCMEC also identified more than 275 direct victims of AI-generated child sexual abuse material during 2024 and 2025. In many cases, the person responsible had direct access to the child. Those reports involve child exploitation rather than cyberbullying alone. However, NCMEC warns that classmates can use AI to create fake images and videos for bullying.

The content can circulate through schools and cause severe emotional harm. AI fakes may also be used for blackmail or sextortion. Parents should never dismiss an altered image because it is fake. The humiliation can feel painfully real. Copies may also keep circulating after the original post disappears. A child may fear that teachers, classmates or future friends will believe the image is genuine.
Tips for talking to kids about cyberbullying
One serious lecture will not prepare a child for every app, friend or group chat. Instead, return to this conversation as your child's online habits change. These steps can help you begin.

Opening with "You spend too much time on that phone" will probably lead to an argument. Ask which game they have been playing. Find out what their friends are sharing. You could also ask whether a group chat has started feeling uncomfortable or stressful.

The goal is to understand where your child spends time online. You probably know the names of their closest school friends. Try to learn about the people they interact with online too. That interest can make it easier for a child to describe a problem later.

Children need examples they can recognize. A joke becomes harmful when the person asks for it to stop and the group keeps going. Sharing someone's picture without permission can also cross a boundary.

Spreading a rumor or creating a fake account to embarrass someone can cause lasting harm. Ask your child whether they would make the same comment with the other person sitting beside them. That pause may stop an impulsive post from growing into a much bigger problem.
Many children stay silent because they fear losing access to their device. Tell your child that showing you a troubling message will not automatically lead to punishment.

You may eventually need to restrict an app or change how the device is used. However, your first response should focus on what happened and whether the child feels safe. Listen before contacting another family. When possible, explain what you plan to do next. A child is more likely to keep talking when they feel included in the response.

An angry reply can create another screenshot for people to share. Tell your child to stop responding when an exchange becomes heated. They can mute the conversation and show the device to a trusted adult. They should also avoid forwarding the content.

Even a reaction emoji can keep the post active and encourage more children to join. Federal bullying guidance advises children not to reply to or forward cyberbullying messages. It also recommends blocking threatening or questionable accounts.
The first instinct may be to erase a cruel post immediately. Take screenshots first. Capture the username, date and complete conversation.

Save emails, links and text messages. Write down when the behavior happened and whether anyone else saw it. You can use that evidence when reporting the account to the platform or school. StopBullying.gov recommends saving screenshots, emails and messages before reporting cyberbullying.

After saving the evidence, block the person responsible. Report the post through the app or platform. Choose the category that most accurately describes what happened. If students from the same school are involved, contact an administrator and ask for the school's cyberbullying policy.

Tell the school what you already reported to the platform. Share enough evidence to explain the situation without spreading the harmful content further. Direct threats or stalking may require contacting law enforcement. Seek emergency help when anyone faces immediate danger.
Make your child's social media accounts private when the platform offers that choice. Review the follower list together. Remove accounts your child does not recognize or no longer trusts.
Check whether posts reveal a school name or regular location. Look for phone numbers and home addresses too. Family members should review their own accounts.

A grandparent may proudly share a school photo without noticing the logo on a uniform. A relative might post a practice schedule or tag the child's exact location. Before sharing, ask what an angry classmate or stranger could learn from the post.
A stolen account can quickly become a cyberbullying tool. Someone may impersonate your child, publish private conversations or send cruel messages to classmates.

Use a different password for every account. A password manager can create and store strong passwords so children do not reuse one login across several apps. Turn on multifactor authentication wherever it is available.

Children should also avoid sharing passwords with friends. Friendships can change, and access given today may be abused after an argument. Check out the best expert-reviewed password managers of 2026 at CyberGuy.com.
STUDY FINDS MORE AI PRAISE FOR BLACK STUDENTS, SOFTER TREATMENT OF FEMALES
AI tools have raised the stakes for cyberbullying by making it easier to create fake images, cloned voices and convincing videos targeting children. (AP Photo/Kiichiro Sato, File)

Require children to ask before installing an unofficial gaming client, mod or computer program. A convincing video can promote a download that hides malware. Once installed, malicious software may steal passwords or allow someone to access private files.
Tell children never to disable security software because an online creator says a warning is harmless. They should download mods only from established communities recognized by the game's developer.

Strong antivirus software can help detect malicious files and block dangerous websites. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.

Parental controls can help manage app downloads, content access and time spent on a device. Apple's Screen Time allows parents to set app limits and restrict certain content on a child's iPhone or iPad.

Google Family Link can manage apps and set screen-time limits on supported Android devices and Chromebooks. Microsoft Family Safety includes screen-time settings and content filters across supported devices. Some web filtering features require Microsoft Edge.
Tell children which controls you use and why. Secret monitoring can damage trust. A child who understands the rules has a better chance of respecting the boundaries.
You can also review my top child monitoring programs if built-in settings do not provide enough support at CyberGuy.com.
Do not tell a child to ignore an explicit deepfake because people know it was created with AI. Save the evidence without forwarding it. Report every account distributing the content.

Contact the school when students are involved. You can also report suspected child sexual exploitation to NCMEC's CyberTipline. Its Take It Down service creates a digital fingerprint of eligible images or videos so participating platforms can detect copies without the image leaving the device.
Do not download or ask someone to send you an explicit image of a minor to make a report. NCMEC specifically warns against downloading or sharing the content for submission.
A bully may send a child their home address or the names of relatives to frighten them. That information could come from public social media posts, people-search websites or data brokers.

Limit the family details you publish publicly. Ask relatives to do the same. A data removal service may reduce the information available through people-search and broker sites. No service can erase every detail, but ongoing removal can make sensitive information harder to locate. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com.

Contact the school when classmates are involved or the online harassment begins affecting attendance. Report credible threats to law enforcement. Seek immediate help when a child appears to be in danger.
Do not try to negotiate with someone who claims to control a child's account, camera or computer. Disconnect the device from the internet. Then run a full security scan.
Change passwords from another device that you know is safe. Most importantly, reassure the child that asking for help was the right decision.
Children notice how adults behave online. They see angry arguments on Facebook. They notice when family members share humiliating memes or attack someone in the comments.
An adult may view that behavior as blowing off steam. A child may see permission to act the same way. Before posting, ask whether you would say those words with your child sitting beside you.

Grandparents can set a powerful example too. They often have close relationships with grandchildren and may hear something a child hesitates to tell a parent. Let your grandchild know they can show you a troubling message without being blamed. Then involve the parents unless doing so could place the child in immediate danger.
Families preparing for the school year can also review my updated best back-to-school supplies and tech for students at CyberGuy.com.
You do not have to wait for a crisis. Send this article to another parent. Share it with grandparents, relatives and anyone who regularly cares for your child.
Then agree on how the adults will respond if a child reports an online problem. A child should hear the same message from every trusted adult: Tell us what happened. We will listen before reacting.
That response may stop a child from hiding something because they fear punishment or embarrassment. It may also give a bystander the confidence to speak up when someone else is being targeted.
Kurt's key takeaways

Cyberbullying may begin with a joke, rumor or altered picture. Within minutes, it can follow a child across several accounts and into the classroom. Recent research shows that many teenagers see harassment as a serious problem on the platforms they use. AI has also made humiliating fake content easier to create and harder to contain. Security tools can protect accounts and devices. Parental controls can create useful boundaries. However, children still need adults who will listen before taking over. Parents and grandparents should keep the conversation going as apps and friendships change. Share these tips with the people who care for the children in your family. Then make sure every child knows which trusted adult they can approach when something feels wrong.

title: Is your Social Security number on the dark web?
summary: A leaked Social Security number can fuel tax fraud, benefits fraud and new account openings. Key warning signs and a credit freeze can limit damage.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.
If you suspect your Social Security number is on the dark web, the right move is not to panic. It is to act quickly, methodically and in the right order.

A leaked Social Security number can be used in ways that go far beyond one fraudulent credit card charge. Criminals may try to open new credit accounts, file fake tax returns, hijack benefits or combine your SSN with other stolen details to impersonate you. The good news is that you can take concrete steps to check for signs of exposure and reduce the damage if your information has already been compromised.
This guide walks through how to check whether your SSN may be exposed, what to do next and how ongoing monitoring can help you catch problems earlier.
