AIR TAXIS CUT HOUR-LONG COMMUTES TO MINUTES, RIDERS MAY BE SHOCKED BY THE PRICE
DoorDash Air plans to use company-built drones to deliver eligible food, medicine and everyday essentials. (DoorDash)
DoorDash becomes a certified air carrier

DoorDash announced the FAA certification on July 29, 2026. The company says it is the eighth drone operator to earn this type of federal air carrier certificate. The FAA uses Part 135 certification for companies that carry other people's property for payment. For drones, it provides the regulatory path for commercial package deliveries beyond a pilot's direct line of sight.

Getting certified requires a five-phase FAA review. The agency evaluates the operator's aircraft, maintenance procedures and safety program. Even after earning the certificate, an operator still needs airspace authorization. It may also need exemptions or waivers for flights beyond visual line of sight. State rules and local land-use requirements can also affect where a delivery hub operates. So, DoorDash has cleared a major federal hurdle. Still, each real-world delivery network will require more planning and approval.
Why DoorDash wants to deliver orders by drone

Anyone who has watched a hot meal slowly travel across town can understand the appeal. DoorDash says more than 20% of its orders in 2025 traveled between three and five miles. Those orders took nearly 25% longer than shorter trips, according to the company.

DoorDash blames part of that delay on the challenge of matching a Dasher with a mid-range order. A driver may prefer several shorter deliveries near a busy restaurant area instead of one longer trip. A drone could take the longer order while a Dasher remains close to restaurants. As a result, the customer could get a faster delivery while the driver moves on to another nearby order.

DoorDash estimates that drone deliveries completed during 2025 took an average of about 25 minutes. The company also says some locations in its partner drone pilots saw order volume rise by roughly 30%. That increase continued during the nine weeks after the pilot began. Those are DoorDash's figures, so performance could change by location, weather and the type of order. Still, they help explain why the company wants more control over the aircraft carrying its deliveries.
CHINESE DRONE MONOPOLY PUT ON NOTICE AMID CONCERNS OVER CCP SPYING: 'STRATEGIC MISTAKE'
DoorDash will continue its partnerships with drone partners like Alphabet's Wing as it designs its own aircraft. (DoorDash)
DoorDash Air will build its own delivery drones
That is the same robotics and autonomy group behind DoorDash's Dot delivery robot.

DoorDash says its drone will be designed and built in the United States. The majority of its components will also come from the U.S., according to the company. DoorDash has not revealed the aircraft's range, payload capacity or final design. A DoorDash spokesperson told CyberGuy that the company plans to share more details about those specifics this fall.
DoorDash drones will work alongside human Dashers

DoorDash says Dashers will continue handling the vast majority of its daily deliveries. That makes sense. A drone cannot walk into an apartment building or carry a large catering order upstairs. It also may struggle with bad weather or a location without a suitable drop zone.
Instead, DoorDash wants its Autonomous Delivery Platform to select the best method for each order. The platform can assign a Dasher. It can also choose an autonomous option such as Dot or a drone.

For example, a small order traveling four miles to a suburban house may fit a drone. A large grocery order going to a high-rise apartment will likely need a person. This approach follows a broader shift across the delivery industry. Uber Eats has also moved toward drone deliveries, while other companies continue testing robots and airborne delivery systems.
What the FAA certification does not guarantee

FAA certification gives DoorDash the legal foundation to operate an air carrier. It does not provide blanket permission to begin unlimited drone flights in every city. DoorDash has not announced its first DoorDash Air markets. The company also has not provided a detailed timeline for deliveries using its in-house aircraft.

In addition, longer autonomous routes may require FAA approval for beyond visual line of sight operations. Local zoning, environmental reviews and community concerns can also shape where hubs are built. Noise could become a major issue. The FAA notes that drone noise may bother a community even when it falls below the level of a significant environmental impact.
Therefore, early service will likely remain limited to carefully selected areas. Suburban neighborhoods with predictable routes and open drop-off spaces may prove easier than dense urban blocks.
JETBLUE FLIGHT REPORTS DRONE STRIKE DURING APPROACH TO NEW YORK AIRPORT: FAA
DoorDash says drones will handle select orders while human Dashers continue making most of the company’s deliveries. (DoorDash)
What this means to you

DoorDash drone delivery could shorten the wait for small, urgent orders. Cold medicine could arrive without waiting for a driver to cross town. A nurse finishing a long shift might get a hot meal faster. A forgotten phone charger could reach you before your battery runs out. However, availability will depend heavily on where you live. Your address may need to fall within an eligible drone delivery zone. The order must also meet the aircraft's weight and size limits. DoorDash told CyberGuy that it is testing the aircraft to operate across a wider range of weather conditions and climates. The company said it will pause operations during extreme weather until conditions return to an operable level.

You should also look closely at the final cost. DoorDash has not said whether its new in-house DoorDash Air service will carry a separate fee or change how tipping works. The company also has not explained whether customers will choose between a DoorDash Air drone and a Dasher once the new service launches. DoorDash's current partner-operated program does allow eligible customers to select drone delivery at checkout.

For now, think of DoorDash Air as an important step toward wider service rather than a nationwide launch. The federal certificate gives DoorDash the regulatory foundation to operate its own commercial drone delivery service. However, individual operations may still require airspace authorization and other FAA approvals. The next test will be whether DoorDash can make drone delivery reliable enough for an ordinary Tuesday night dinner. For more background on how companies are already testing airborne orders, check out how drones are changing food delivery.
Kurt's key takeaways

DoorDash has spent years learning how to move orders through streets. Now it wants to control what happens in the sky. FAA certification gives DoorDash Air a serious start. The company has the app, the restaurant relationships and billions of past orders to study. It also knows where deliveries slow down. Still, building a drone is only one piece of the job. DoorDash must prove that its aircraft can operate safely and consistently. It must also keep food intact while avoiding noise problems and neighborhood resistance. Human Dashers are not disappearing. Instead, DoorDash wants drones and robots to handle specific trips that could be faster without a car.

Would you trust a DoorDash drone to lower dinner into your yard, or would the sound of delivery aircraft flying over your neighborhood ruin the convenience? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: Fake party invitation scam can hijack your computer
summary: Fake party invitations trick victims into downloading malware that gives criminals remote access to computers and spreads through contact lists.
story: Clicking links in a fake party invitation email can install malware that gives criminals remote access to your computer and personal information, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson explains.

You sit down at your computer to clear out your inbox. Then you spot a party invitation from someone you recognize. Maybe it appears to come from a friend. Perhaps the sender belongs to a group you know. Either way, the familiar name makes the message feel safe enough to open.

Inside, everything looks cheerful. There is an envelope graphic, a friendly note and what appears to be an invitation for a wedding or retirement party. However, you cannot see the event details yet. The message tells you to save the invitation or install something to join the guest list.

That request should stop you cold. A legitimate party invitation should not require you to install software before you can see when or where the event takes place. That small download could give a criminal remote access to your computer. Here’s how this fake invitation scam works and what you can do before one click puts your computer and contacts at risk.

You’ll also learn how to curb political texts, clean up your inbox and spot messages that could put your personal information at risk.
Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.
FAKE SHINYHUNTERS SEXTORTION EMAIL USES CARNIVAL BREACH DATA
A fake party invitation can trick recipients into downloading software that gives criminals remote access to a Windows computer. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
How malicious party invitations reach your inbox

The scam begins with trust. An invitation appears to come from someone whose name you recognize, so you become less suspicious. Criminals may copy the look of a legitimate invitation platform. They can add a colorful envelope, an exclusive-sounding message and a button that promises to reveal the details.

The email has one main purpose: getting you to click. Once you press the invitation, the message sends you to a separate website. That page says a friend sent you something and asks you to download a file to view it.
The request may seem simple. Still, party invitations normally open inside a website or app. They do not need to install a program on your computer.
Why the fake invitation page looks convincing

The landing page may contain a large "Download invitation" button. It may also display a familiar company name inside the web address. However, seeing a trusted brand somewhere in a link proves very little. Criminals can place that name inside a much longer address or add extra letters that make the domain look authentic at a glance.

You need to identify the real domain instead of focusing on the first familiar word you see. The page may also create confusion. It could claim that your invitation is already downloading while another message asks you to click if the download fails. Some versions even include a testimonial from a supposed guest who says opening the invitation was easy.

A review on a private party invitation page should feel strange. Those details are designed to quiet your doubts and push you toward the download button. For more visual breakdowns of scams like this, check out The CyberGuy Report podcast at CyberGuy.com.
What happens after you download the fake invitation

In the example we describe, the website directs you to open the file on a Windows computer. That device-specific request is another major warning sign. Why would a party invitation care which device you use? The malicious file may contain a remote access tool. Businesses use legitimate versions of this software to troubleshoot computers from another location.

Criminals can abuse similar tools to control your system without permission. Once you install the file, an attacker may be able to search your computer or access saved information. The exact damage depends on the program and the permissions it receives. Your email account can become an especially valuable target. It contains personal conversations along with a contact list filled with people who trust you.

The criminals can then send the same fake invitation to your friends and relatives. Those people may open it because the message appears to come from your real account. As a result, one compromised computer can start a chain reaction.
Why these invitation scams keep working

People receive a steady stream of spam, fake alerts and impersonation attempts. Criminals can also use AI tools to create cleaner writing and more realistic designs. That makes the familiar sender name even more powerful.

You may be cautious around a message from a stranger. Yet you might act quickly when the invitation appears to come from someone you know. The scam succeeds when familiarity replaces verification. Email providers and technology companies continue to improve their filters. Even so, dangerous messages still reach real inboxes. That leaves you making the final decision about whether a link deserves your trust.
HOTEL WI-FI PHISHING ATTACK TARGETS MICROSOFT LOGINS
Scam emails may appear to come from a trusted contact and use cheerful invitation graphics to make a malicious download seem legitimate. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Tips to stay safe from fake party invitation scams
A few precautions can help you recognize a malicious invitation before it compromises your computer or accounts.

Use strong antivirus software and keep it actively running in the background on your devices. Real-time protection can warn you about a dangerous link or block a malicious download before it reaches your computer.

If you clicked the invitation or downloaded a suspicious file, delete the file without opening it and run a full security scan. A scan can help identify unwanted software that may have reached your computer. Keep your operating system, browser and security software updated as well. Updates often close weaknesses that criminals try to exploit. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com

Stop immediately if an invitation tells you to download or install a program before you can see the event. Real invitation services normally show the details in your browser or inside their official app. You should not need a separate installer. Delete the message instead of trying to see what happens next.

On a computer, place your cursor over a link without pressing it. Your browser or email program should reveal the destination address. Read the entire address carefully. Watch for misspellings, unexpected words or extra letters added around a legitimate company name. A familiar logo does not confirm that the link belongs to the real company.

Avoid using the link inside the email when you have doubts. Instead, type the invitation service's web address into your browser or open its official app. Sign in and look for the invitation there. If it does not appear in your account, the email may be fake.

Reach out through a separate text message or phone call if an invitation feels unusual. Do not reply directly to the suspicious email. A criminal may control the sender's account or may have forged the address. Ask whether the person actually sent the invitation and whether it requires a download.
FAKE PASSWORD-MANAGER ALERTS COULD PUT YOUR VAULT AT RISK
Legitimate digital invitations should not require users to install software before viewing an event’s date, location or guest information. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)

Your risk is generally lower if you visited the page but did not run anything. Close the browser tab without pressing the download button. If the file has already downloaded, leave it closed and delete it. Opening the file gives the malicious program a chance to run. Never open it simply to find out what it contains.

Use your email provider's Report phishing option before deleting the invitation. Reporting the message can help the provider block similar emails and warn other recipients. You can also block the sender if you do not recognize the address.

A data removal service can help remove your details from many public data broker databases. This may make it harder for scammers to find personal information they can use to make a message feel convincing. However, no service can remove every record. It also cannot prevent a criminal from reaching you through a compromised friend's contact list. Still, reducing your public exposure can give scammers less material to work with. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com.

Turn on two-factor authentication (2FA) for your email account. This adds another barrier if criminals steal or guess your password. Never approve an unexpected login request. Also, do not share a security code with anyone who contacts you.

If you typed your email address, password or security code into the fake page, use a clean device to change that password immediately. Change it anywhere else you reused it. Then review the account for unfamiliar activity, new recovery information or settings you did not change. Use a password manager to create and store a strong, unique password for every account so one stolen login cannot unlock several services.

Disconnect the computer from the internet if you ran the installer or noticed unexpected remote activity. Next, run a full security scan. You may also need help from a trusted computer professional to confirm that the remote access software is gone. Use a different, clean device to change important passwords. Start with your email account because criminals may use it to reset passwords for other services. Also, review your email account for unfamiliar forwarding rules or active login sessions. Warn your contacts if suspicious messages may have gone out under your name.
Kurt's key takeaways

A party invitation should give you information, not demand access to your computer. Delete the message if it asks you to install anything before revealing the event. Check the full destination of every link. Then contact the supposed sender separately when something feels unusual. If you downloaded a file but did not open it, delete it and run a security scan. If you ran the file, disconnect the computer and secure your accounts from a clean device. Most importantly, pay attention to that moment when something feels off. A few seconds of doubt can stop a criminal from getting inside your computer. Want to see more? Check out The CyberGuy Report podcast.

title: The scam text test: Spot danger before you tap
summary: A simple six-step scam text test helps you spot phishing messages about fake deliveries, toll notices and bank alerts before you click or share anything.
story: Halimah Delaine Prado, Google General Counsel, reveals the rise of AI-powered phishing scams originating from China's 'outsider enterprise.' She explains how these criminals use artificial intelligence to create highly convincing fake websites, impersonating trusted brands like T-Mobile to defraud hundreds of thousands of Americans, causing millions in losses. Prado highlights Google's strategy to combat these evolving threats.

Your phone buzzes. The text reads, "Your package is delayed. Confirm your address here." A little later, it's a text message about an unpaid toll, suspicious bank activity or an account that will be locked unless you act now.

That's how scam texts work. They don't always look wild or obviously fake. They look routine, urgent and easy to deal with in a hurry. The good news: You don't need to memorize every scam. You just need a quick way to test suspicious messages before you tap. Here's the simple scam text test to run before you click, pay or share anything.

Scam texts often imitate delivery companies, banks, toll agencies and online services to pressure people into clicking dangerous links. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
The scam text test
If a text asks you to click, pay, verify, sign in or fix a problem, run through these checks first.

Are you actually waiting for that package? Do you use that bank? Did you recently drive on a toll road? If the answer is no, treat the message as suspicious. Even if the answer is yes, don't assume it's real. Scammers rely on coincidence. They send thousands of similar messages knowing that some recipients will be waiting for a package or use the company being impersonated.
Urgency is one of the biggest red flags. Watch for phrases like:

A real company may send an urgent alert, but scammers use pressure to stop you from checking whether the message is legitimate. Take a breath before responding. A few extra minutes spent verifying the message can prevent days or weeks of dealing with a stolen account.
Before tapping, check for:

Even if the address looks legitimate, avoid opening links in unexpected texts. Scammers can disguise links or create convincing copies of real websites. Verify the message through the company's official app or a website you type in yourself.

Many scam texts use vague greetings, odd wording, awkward punctuation or slightly incorrect brand names. You might see a message addressed to "Dear customer" instead of your name. It may refer to a package without showing an order number or claim to come from a bank without identifying the account involved. Good grammar doesn't guarantee a message is safe. Scammers now use artificial intelligence to write more convincing messages. Still, sloppy wording and missing details remain warning signs.

Legitimate companies may send you a one-time verification code. However, a bank, government agency or customer service representative should never ask you to give that code to someone else. Anyone who asks for your code may be trying to take control of your account.
This is the most important step. Instead of using the link or phone number in the message:

If the issue is real, you should still be able to find it through one of those trusted channels.
FAKE PASSWORD-MANAGER ALERTS COULD PUT YOUR VAULT AT RISK
A quick scam text checklist can help users spot fake alerts before sharing passwords, payment details or one-time security codes. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
What scam texts usually look like
Scam texts often fall into a few familiar categories.

These messages claim a package was delayed, an address needs to be corrected or a small shipping fee must be paid. The link may lead to a fake postal or delivery website that collects your card information, password or home address.

These texts claim someone used your card, your account has been locked or you must verify a transaction immediately. The message may include a phone number connecting you to a scammer pretending to work for the bank.

Toll scams claim you owe a small amount and will face a larger penalty if you don't pay immediately. The amount is often low enough to make paying seem easier than investigating. The payment page then steals your financial information.

These messages claim your email, payment app, streaming service or social media account will be suspended. They direct you to a fake login page designed to capture your username and password. These scams work because each message sounds plausible. The goal is to make you react first and think later.

How antivirus software can help

Good habits are your first line of defense, but strong antivirus software can add another layer of protection. Some security tools can warn you about suspicious links, phishing websites and malicious downloads before they put your information at risk.

Many text scams are only the first step. The message sends you to a fake website. That site may steal your password, payment details or other personal information. In some cases, it may also try to install malware on your device.
Look for security software that offers:

Protection against phishing websites and dangerous linksReal-time scanning for malware, ransomware and spywareScam detection for suspicious messages and websitesPassword management toolsFirewall protectionAlerts when your personal information appears in a data breach

Security software cannot catch every scam or replace careful judgment. Still, it can help stop a suspicious link or malicious download before one quick tap leads to fraud or an account takeover. Features vary by provider and device, so check what is included before choosing a service.

The one rule to remember
You never have to solve a surprise text from inside the text. Stop, verify independently and only act through official channels. That one habit can help you avoid a huge number of text scams.
Kurt's key takeaways

Scam texts work because they make an everyday problem feel urgent. A package delay, unpaid toll or bank warning can seem believable enough to make you tap without thinking. Don't use the link or phone number in the message. Open the company's official app, type its website yourself or call a number you already trust. Strong antivirus software can help flag some suspicious texts and fake websites, but no security tool catches everything. Taking a few seconds to verify the message can save you from a stolen account or a costly mistake.

title: Water cyberattack hits at least 7 states
summary: CISA warned about exposed programmable logic controllers weeks before hackers targeted dozens of Minnesota water utilities in a coordinated strike.
story: National correspondent Madeleine Rivera reports on the federal investigation into a cyberattack targeting community water systems in Minnesota and at least six other states. Federal agencies including the FBI, CISA, and the EPA warn that Iran-affiliated threat actors are targeting critical infrastructure. The segment outlines the national security implications of these cyber threats on local utility systems.

You probably never think about the computer systems behind your kitchen faucet. You turn the handle and expect clean water. That familiar routine suddenly felt far less certain in Minnesota and six other states.

A coordinated cyberattack targeted operational technology at more than 30 community water systems on Sunday, July 26, and Monday, July 27. Minnesota IT Services, known as MNIT, activated the state's cybersecurity response and brought in federal agencies to help investigate.

One water plant temporarily went offline. Meanwhile, other communities reported problems involving automated controls or communications equipment. Workers switched to manual operations or used backup procedures to keep essential services running. Fortunately, state officials reported no active requests for residents to reduce or change their drinking water use.
The FBI has since said that water or wastewater utility companies in seven states have been affected.
"Some of that activity degraded water operations," the bureau said.
This water cyberattack raises an uncomfortable question for towns across America. How many local utilities could keep operating if hackers gained access to the computers controlling their equipment?
INVESTIGATORS BELIEVE IRANIAN HACKERS ARE LIKELY BEHIND CYBERATTACK ON MINNESOTA WATER SYSTEMS: REPORT

Our free CyberGuy Live class, "Sick of Spam?," has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our spam-stopping checklist. A water tower is seen Thursday, July 30, 2026, in Plymouth, Minn. A cyberattack targeted operating technology at more than 30 water systems in Minnesota, including Plymouth's, earlier this week, state officials said. (Ellen Schmidt/AP)
What happened in the Minnesota water cyberattack

The attack targeted operational technology, commonly called OT. These systems control physical equipment such as pumps, valves and treatment machinery. In Braham, city officials initially reported that the water plant had gone offline for an unknown reason. Crews restored the facility within hours and said it was again filtering and treating water as expected.

Officials later blamed the outage on a malicious cyberattack against computerized operating systems. The city relied on water already stored in its tower while crews worked on the problem. Plymouth reported communications problems involving two water towers and several wastewater lift stations. However, officials said water levels and water quality remained unaffected.

South St. Paul also identified a cybersecurity incident involving automated water utility controls. Public Works employees used established contingency procedures to maintain normal water and wastewater operations. Maple Plain publicly confirmed that its water utility technology had also been targeted.

In total, four communities have publicly described specific effects, although MNIT says attackers targeted more than 30 systems statewide. That difference is important. Being targeted does not mean every system suffered a shutdown. However, it shows that someone tried to reach a large number of local utilities within a short period.
Who may be behind the Minnesota water cyberattack

Officials have not announced a definitive attribution. However, a July 30 report from The New York Times says investigators preliminarily believe Iranian hackers were probably responsible. The report cited U.S. and state officials familiar with the investigation, but President Donald Trump said he rejected the suggestion that Iran was behind the breaches.

Those officials cautioned that the assessment could change as investigators collect more technical evidence. They also have not ruled out the possibility that attackers tried to make the activity appear Iranian. Therefore, Iran should be described as the leading preliminary suspicion rather than the confirmed attacker.

The timing has drawn attention because CISA warned in April that Iranian-affiliated hackers were targeting internet-exposed programmable logic controllers. These devices help control machinery and other equipment at water systems and additional critical infrastructure facilities. CISA initially highlighted certain Rockwell Automation and Allen-Bradley controllers. On July 22, the agency expanded its warning to include equipment from Schneider Electric, Siemens and potentially other manufacturers.

Still, federal officials have not publicly tied that campaign to the Minnesota incidents. CyberGuy has previously examined Iran's expanding cyber threat to U.S. critical infrastructure. Water systems remain attractive targets because even a limited disruption can create fear far beyond the equipment involved.
IRAN-LINKED HACKERS TARGET US MEDICAL TECH COMPANY
A coordinated cyberattack reached operational technology at dozens of Minnesota water systems, exposing security risks for smaller utilities nationwide. (City of St. Cloud)
Why water system cyberattacks threaten U.S. communities

Minnesota's experience could happen in any state. The United States has close to 170,000 drinking water and wastewater systems. Many now connect physical equipment to internet-enabled technology so workers can monitor facilities from a distance. That remote access helps utilities manage equipment spread across wide service areas. However, it may also give an attacker a route into vital controls when operators fail to secure the connection.

Smaller communities often face the greatest challenge. The Government Accountability Office says water systems have widely different cybersecurity capabilities. Many also use older technology that can be difficult to update. At the same time, utilities must stretch limited budgets across essential repairs and regulatory requirements. Cybersecurity upgrades may compete with work that residents can see, such as replacing aging equipment.

A large utility may employ dedicated security professionals. A small town may rely on plant operators who already handle daily operations and after-hours problems. As a result, the communities with fewer resources may also have less ability to monitor suspicious activity around the clock.

Foreign governments have already shown interest in those weak spots. CyberGuy previously reported how Chinese hackers gained access to critical American systems, including infrastructure connected to water and energy. The attacker may change. The underlying weakness often looks familiar: exposed equipment, outdated technology or remote access that lacks strong protection.
Could a cyberattack make drinking water unsafe?

A cyberattack against a water utility does not automatically mean the water has been contaminated. In Minnesota, officials reported no known impact on drinking water quality. They also told residents in publicly identified communities that normal water use could continue.

However, a successful attack can cause more serious consequences. The EPA warns that hackers could disrupt treatment or damage equipment. In a worst-case situation, attackers might also interfere with processes that protect water quality.

Manual operations can provide an important safety net. Minnesota workers used those procedures to keep systems running while investigators examined affected technology. Still, a manual backup only helps when employees know how to use it. Utilities need to test those procedures before screens go dark and alarms stop reporting correctly.
How CISA says water utilities should strengthen security

CISA published new international guidance on July 28 called "CI Fortify: Advice for Isolating Vital Systems." The guidance urges critical infrastructure operators to separate vital operational technology from less trusted networks. That isolation can help an essential service continue operating when another part of the organization becomes compromised.

CISA released the guidance on the same day MNIT publicly announced the statewide attack. However, the agency has not said it created the document in response to Minnesota. For water utilities, stronger protection may begin with removing unnecessary internet exposure. When remote access remains necessary, CISA advises placing security controls in front of programmable controllers.

Utilities should also change factory passwords and give employees separate login credentials. EPA inspectors have found water systems that continued using default passwords. Inspectors also discovered shared staff accounts or access that remained active after employees left.

Another EPA finding needs careful context. The agency says more than 70% of inspected systems violated basic federal risk assessment or emergency response planning requirements. That figure does not mean 70% had confirmed cybersecurity breaches. However, inspectors found serious digital security weaknesses at some of those facilities.
TRUMP REJECTS IRAN BLAME FOR MINNESOTA CYBERATTACK, POINTS FINGER AT 'CORRUPT' POLITICAL FOE
Hackers targeted computerized controls at more than 30 Minnesota water systems, forcing some utilities to use manual operations and backup procedures. (Tony Webster/Wikimedia Commons)
What to do if your water utility reports a cyberattack
Residents cannot secure a municipal treatment plant themselves. However, a few steps can help you receive reliable information and avoid scams during an incident.

Check your city, county health department or water utility website for updates. Officials will tell you whether you need to reduce water use or boil tap water. Avoid making decisions based on an unverified neighborhood post.

A cyberattack may affect communications or automated equipment without changing water quality. Continue normal use unless local officials provide different instructions. However, follow any boil-water notice immediately if one appears.

Your city may use text messages, automated calls or government phone alerts during a service disruption. Take a moment to check the emergency alert settings on your iPhone or Android. Also, sign up for your city's local notification system if one is available.

A backup supply can help during any water interruption, whether it begins with a cyberattack or equipment failure. The CDC recommends storing at least one gallon of water per person each day for three days. Households may need more for pets or people with medical needs.

Scammers often take advantage of outages and breaking news. You may receive a message claiming that your water bill failed or that your service will be disconnected. Another message may offer bottled water assistance through a payment link. Do not use the phone number or link inside an unexpected message. Instead, contact the utility through its official website or the number printed on your bill. CyberGuy has also explained how scammers impersonate water and other utility companies by spoofing familiar phone numbers.
Kurt's key takeaways

Minnesota contained a troubling attack without a known drinking water emergency. Workers restored Braham's plant while other utilities relied on manual controls or contingency procedures. However, the number of systems targeted should get the attention of every governor and mayor in America. Hackers apparently found a way to reach dozens of local utilities during the same two-day period. The preliminary suspicion involving Iranian hackers also raises the stakes. Still, investigators need more evidence before anyone treats that attribution as settled. Every community should know which water controls face the internet and whether workers can operate essential equipment manually. States should also help smaller towns that cannot afford their own cybersecurity teams.
How confident are you that your community could handle a cyberattack on its water system, and what would you want local officials to tell you first? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

title: Kentucky middle school teacher accused of crossing the line with student, arrested under new anti-grooming law
summary: Sadie M. Flores faces grooming a minor charges under a Kentucky law that took effect just weeks before her arrest at Graves County Middle School.
story: Fox News Digital spoke with attorney Wendy Murphy about a recently released independent report on the decades of sexual abuse at Miss Hall's School in Pittsfield, Massachusetts.

A Kentucky middle school teacher is facing serious criminal charges after allegations involving a student exposed conduct that crossed the line from inappropriate to criminal, according to authorities.
Sadie M. Flores, 25, of Mayfield, was arrested Friday afternoon and charged with grooming a minor, a Class D felony under a Kentucky law that took effect just weeks ago on July 15.
According to the Graves County Sheriff's Office, Flores, an employee at Graves County Middle School, is accused of having an improper relationship with a minor student in the district.
TEACHER WHO SERVED AS GOP STATE LAWMAKER ALLEGEDLY USED ROBLOX TO LURE STUDENT INTO SEXUAL RELATIONSHIP
Authorities arrested Graves County Middle School teacher Sadie Flores after an investigation into an alleged improper relationship with a student. (Graves County Detention Center)
The allegations were first reported to Graves County Schools, whose administrators immediately notified the Graves County Sheriff's Office, prompting a criminal investigation.

Detectives said the investigation included the seizure of electronic records, interviews and other investigative measures. Flores was interviewed Friday afternoon before being taken into custody around 3:30 p.m.
She was booked into the Graves County Restricted Custody Center before later being transferred to an out-of-county detention facility.
Sheriff Jon Hayden said the investigation remains ongoing.
HIGH SCHOOL COUNSELOR PLEADS GUILTY TO MULTIPLE SEX CRIMES INVOLVING TEEN SHE WAS MEANT TO HELP
Authorities arrested Sadie Flores after an investigation into allegations involving a student. (Graves County Sheriff's Office)
Graves County Schools Superintendent Matt Madding said district leaders immediately contacted law enforcement after learning of the allegations.

"District administration was made aware of an allegation involving a teacher at Graves County Middle School. School officials immediately reported this information to the Graves County Sheriff's Department for investigation," Madding said in a statement.
"We have since been informed that, as a result of that investigation, charges have been filed against this teacher."
Because the investigation and personnel matter remain ongoing, Madding said the district is limited in what it can publicly discuss but emphasized that student safety remains its top priority.
FORMER CHRISTIAN SCHOOL TEACHER SENTENCED AFTER PLEADING GUILTY TO CHILD SEDUCTION CHARGE
Graves County Middle School in Mayfield, Kentucky, where Sadie Flores was employed before her arrest. (Graves County Middle School)

"We take any allegation involving the safety of a child or the professional conduct of an employee extremely seriously and will continue to cooperate fully with law enforcement and the appropriate authorities," he said.

The grooming charge stems from a Kentucky law that took effect July 15, creating a new felony offense aimed at adults accused of cultivating inappropriate relationships with minors before sexual abuse occurs.

Authorities have not released additional details about the alleged relationship, the student's age, or whether additional charges could be filed as the investigation continues.

title: North Dakota mom stabs her 2 children to death in 'horrific' killing that left cops traumatized: officials
summary: A North Dakota mother faces murder and attempted murder charges after allegedly stabbing her 5-month-old and 3-year-old to death in a home attack.
story: New York City crime policies face intense scrutiny after 12-year-old Jacob Freytes is killed by a stray bullet in the Bronx. Mother Migdalia Martinez and sister Angelica Coriano join 'Fox & Friends' to speak out, demanding justice and slamming the suspect's lengthy arrest record. Martinez warns that career criminals currently feel more safe than ever before.
This story discusses suicide. If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 988 or 1-800-273-TALK (8255).
A North Dakota mother is accused of stabbing two of her children to death in what police described as a "horrific" attack that left even officers traumatized by the sight of the bloody scene.
Kailey Erhart, 22, stabbed her 5-month-old and 3-year-old children to death on Thursday after waving a gun at her estranged husband and threatening to kill herself, according to police.
Her 1-year-old child survived the attack, but suffered serious injuries. The child underwent surgery, but police have not released the latest medical status.
Mandan Police Chief Jason Ziegler said the crime scene was likely one of the most horrific things his officers will ever see.
CALIFORNIA MOM BEGGED FOR HELP BEFORE EX GUNNED HER DOWN IN FRONT OF THEIR 4-YEAR-OLD SON: DA
Kailey Erhart, 22, stabbed her 5-month-old and 3-year-old children to death and injured her 1-year-old: police. (Burleigh County Detention Center)

"A scene like that is something that nobody should ever have to see, and the way [the officers] came through in one of the most horrific times that they’ll probably experience in their life, I’m proud," Mandan Police Chief Jason Ziegler said at a press conference.

"I want to acknowledge this is an extreme, tragic and heartbreaking incident for the children involved, their families, our community and first responders who arrived on scene," he added. "Our thoughts are with everyone that were impacted."
The kids' father, who intended to file for divorce, was at home with their children when police were alerted that Erhart was threatening to end her own life, KFYR reported.

Earlier that day, Erhart threatened her husband with a gun she had recently purchased, but he was able to disarm her during a physical struggle, take the gun apart and scatter the pieces. Erhart bit and scratched him during the struggle, according to the report.
JUDGE SENTENCES NEVADA MOM FOR DROWNING YOUNG SON, DAUGHTER: 'I WILL REMEMBER YOUR CASE FOREVER'
Kailey Erhart faces nine charges, including two counts of murder, one count of attempted murder and multiple counts of aggravated assault and terrorizing. (GoFundMe)
The children’s grandmother was at the home when the killings happened, telling police that Erhart chased her and the kids' father out of the house with a knife before the alleged slayings.
Erhart faces nine charges, including two counts of murder, one count of attempted murder and multiple counts of aggravated assault and terrorizing.
A judge set Erhart’s cash bond at $3 million, highlighting "the extreme violence in these alleged charges and the threat to the community, victims, and children," according to KFYR.
The court also issued formal no-contact orders barring Erhart from contacting the surviving victims or family members.
The 1-year-old child survived the attack, but suffered serious injuries. (GoFundMe)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Erhart's preliminary hearing and arraignment are set for October 6.
A GoFundMe created to support the children and their father has raised more than $25,000 as of Sunday night.

"He is a father trying to survive something no parent should ever have to face," the fundraiser created by the man's mother reads. "I lost two precious souls in a devastating tragedy after they were murdered by their mother, and the pain is more than I can put into words. Every day, we are carrying unimaginable grief while also trying to stay strong for his surviving child, who is receiving ongoing medical care and facing challenges no child should ever have to endure."

title: Teen burglary ring linked to nearly 80 Bay Area break-ins dismantled after months-long investigation: PD
summary: Surveillance video shows teenage suspects pointing a stolen firearm at a garage door, waiting for a homeowner during a brazen Bay Area burglary spree.
story: Concord police surveillance video shows suspects breaking into vehicles, entering residential garages with stolen garage door openers and carrying out a Bay Area burglary spree. Credit: Concord Police Department

A gang of teenage burglars accused of targeting nearly 80 Bay Area homes and vehicles is behind bars after investigators unraveled a months-long crime spree that included stolen firearms, high-speed chases and an alleged fencing operation that netted roughly $250,000 in suspected stolen property.
Concord police also released surveillance video of the burglary spree, dubbing the compilation "Teamwork Leads to Arrests in Regional Armed Burglary Series."

The video shows the suspects breaking into parked vehicles in the early morning hours before using stolen garage door openers to gain access to attached garages, where investigators said they stole power tools, firearms and other valuables.
NEW WARRANTS EXPOSE CHILLING, DISTURBING DETAILS IN GREG BIFFLE HOME BURGLARY
Surveillance video released by Concord police shows an armed burglary suspect pointing a firearm toward a home's interior door during the investigation. (Concord Police Department)

In one of the most brazen moments captured on camera, investigators said the suspects pointed a firearm at the interior door connecting a garage to a home, apparently waiting for a homeowner to emerge. During another burglary, the crew allegedly stole 14 firearms from a single residential garage.

By the time the investigation wrapped up, detectives had linked the suspects to 37 vehicle and residential burglaries in Concord and approximately 40 more across Contra Costa and Solano counties. Police said the group also stole multiple vehicles, which they allegedly used to commit additional crimes.
The suspects repeatedly slipped away from officers as the burglary spree unfolded.
In May, an officer spotted a possible suspect vehicle and attempted a traffic stop, but the driver allegedly sped away. Police launched a pursuit before calling it off over public safety concerns.
OREGON BURGLARY SUSPECT NABBED AFTER CRASHING SUV DURING POLICE CHASE: VIDEO
Two burglary suspects break into a parked pickup truck before allegedly using a stolen garage door opener to access nearby homes in California. (Concord Police Department)
During another string of burglaries in June, officers located a different suspect vehicle, but the suspects again escaped.
Later that month, the juveniles allegedly fled another burglary, crashed a vehicle and ran from the scene on foot. They evaded capture once again, though officers recovered a firearm.
The break in the case came in late June, when Concord detectives working with the Richmond Police Department identified four juveniles believed to be behind the burglary spree.
One suspect was already being held in juvenile hall in connection with an unrelated case. Investigators then obtained arrest and search warrants for the remaining three.
Police said the suspects targeted parked vehicles before using stolen garage door openers to enter residential garages. (Concord Police Department)

In July, the Concord Police Department SWAT Team executed simultaneous warrants with assistance from the Antioch Police Department, Pittsburg Police Department, Central County SWAT and the U.S. Marshals Service.
All three outstanding suspects were arrested.

Searches of their residences led to the recovery of two firearms stolen during the burglaries, police said. A third stolen firearm had previously been recovered by the Richmond Police Department during a separate investigation.
As detectives dug deeper, they uncovered what prosecutors describe as an organized fencing operation.
CHICAGO POL SAYS WALGREENS SHOULD BE CHARGED WITH 'FIRST-DEGREE CORPORATE ABANDONMENT' OVER CLOSURE OVER THEFT
Surveillance video released by Concord police shows a masked burglary suspect during a string of home and vehicle break-ins across the Bay Area. (Concord Police Department)

Investigators identified 37-year-old Wuillian Cordova-Cubias of Oakland as the alleged buyer of stolen property, accusing him of purchasing power tools from the juvenile suspects, often shortly after the burglaries occurred.
On Aug. 5, detectives with the Concord Police Department, Oakland Police Department and the U.S. Marshals Service executed a search warrant at Cordova-Cubias' Oakland home.

Police said the search uncovered what investigators believe was the hub of a regional fencing operation. Inside, detectives found at least 500 suspected stolen power tools, along with a stolen ATV, a stolen forklift, an unregistered firearm and numerous other high-value items. Authorities estimated the recovered property was worth approximately $250,000.

The Contra Costa County District Attorney's Office charged Cordova-Cubias with receiving stolen property, two counts of receiving stolen motor vehicles, unlawful firearm activity and conspiracy with juvenile co-conspirators. Prosecutors also filed sentencing enhancements that could increase any potential penalties if he is convicted.
Exterior of the Contra Costa County District Attorney's Office in Martinez, California, where charges were filed in the burglary investigation. (Contra Costa County District Attorney's Office)

"As organized theft offenses have increased, my office has responded by building an effective Organized Theft Unit that works closely with law enforcement to file strong cases we believe we can prove beyond a reasonable doubt in court," Contra Costa County District Attorney Diana Becton said in a statement. "Concord Police Department's thorough investigation into these burglaries and the fencing operation reflects the kind of collaboration that holds individuals accountable."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Cordova-Cubias remains in custody at the Martinez Detention Facility and is scheduled to be arraigned Monday afternoon in Contra Costa County Superior Court.
The Contra Costa County District Attorney's Office also filed complaints against the three juvenile suspects. Their identities have not been released under California law.

title: Indian national accused of Arizona girlfriend's murder entered US on student visa: federal sources
summary: Varun Batchigari allegedly strangled Julissa Salazar near the University of Arizona, then boarded a flight to India before the FBI had him arrested.
story: Jose Medina-Medina, accused of murdering Loyola student Sheridan Gorman, now faces new federal charges for illegal weapon possession within Cook County Jail. Gorman's grieving family recounts his emotionless gaze during the court proceedings, emphasizing the planned nature of her murder. This case highlights ongoing concerns about justice for victims.
The man accused of murdering his teenage girlfriend in Arizona allegedly tried to cover his tracks, flee the country and vanish overseas.

Federal law enforcement sources told Fox News the accused killer, 20-year-old Varun Batchigari, is an Indian national who entered the United States through Los Angeles International Airport on Jan. 8, 2024, on an F-1 student visa.
After the alleged killing, authorities say Batchigari boarded a flight from Houston bound for India with a layover in Germany, where he was arrested after the FBI alerted local authorities.
MIGRANT WHO FLED IRELAND AFTER AMERICAN MOTHER'S MURDER IS ARRESTED IN JORDAN

Varun Batchigari is charged with first-degree murder in the death of 19-year-old Julissa Salazar. Federal law enforcement sources told Fox News he entered the U.S. on an F-1 student visa and was arrested in Germany after allegedly attempting to flee to India. (CBP)
The FBI is now working to extradite him back to Arizona to face a first-degree murder charge.
Batchigari is charged with murdering his 19-year-old girlfriend, Julissa Salazar, who Tucson police say was strangled Thursday inside an off-campus apartment near the University of Arizona.

Investigators allege Batchigari stole Salazar's cellphone and credit cards after the killing, then sent a series of text messages to her mother while posing as the victim in an apparent attempt to conceal the crime. The messages raised concern among Salazar's family, prompting a welfare check that led officers to discover her body.
A felony warrant paints a picture of escalating violence, a deteriorating relationship and mounting personal troubles in the months leading up to Salazar's death.
FITNESS TRAINER TOLD FRIEND SHE WAS 'SCARED FOR HER LIFE' WEEKS BEFORE BODY WITH MATCHING CLOTHING FOUND
Tuscon Police vehicle (Tucscon Police)
According to the warrant, obtained by KOLD-TV, Batchigari had previously been involved in an assault case investigated by the University of Arizona Police Department.

Witnesses interviewed by investigators said Salazar moved out after experiencing problems with Batchigari in late 2025 and had planned to end the relationship because of an alleged history of domestic violence.

The warrant also includes allegations from multiple witnesses describing prior violent behavior. One witness told investigators Batchigari sexually assaulted her at a Halloween party but said she never reported the allegation to law enforcement.

Another witness told investigators Batchigari had been expelled from the University of Arizona following a fight and later lost his job, leading to financial problems and concerns about his student visa status and ability to pay rent.
EXCLUSIVE: DHS SEEKS CUSTODY OF ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT CHARGED WITH MURDER AFTER TRUMP DEPORTATION, BIDEN RELEASE

U.S. border patrol agent Alessio Faccin walks along the border fence separating Mexico from the United States near Calexico, California, U.S. February 8, 2017. Picture taken February 8, 2017. REUTERS/Mike Blake - RC166A17F9D0 (Mike Blake/Reuters)
Federal records reviewed by Fox News show Batchigari remained in lawful immigration status at the time of the alleged murder despite his reported expulsion from the University of Arizona.
Because international students on F-1 visas are generally required to remain enrolled to maintain their legal status, it is unclear why his immigration status had not yet changed.

A Tucson Police Department spokesperson told Fox News Digital there were no updates beyond the information already released publicly. Fox News Digital also reached out to the University of Arizona to confirm Batchigari's enrollment history and whether Salazar was a student, but did not immediately receive a response.

title: Police nab 'armed and dangerous' New York fugitive suspected of killing father and torching home
summary: Thomas David Ryan was captured in Schoharie County after a multiday New York manhunt involving the FBI in his father's homicide and arson case.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

An "armed and dangerous" New York fugitive suspected of killing his 70-year-old father and setting the family home ablaze was captured Sunday, ending a multiday manhunt that drew in the FBI and police agencies across the state.

Thomas David Ryan, 32, was taken into custody in the Gilboa area of Schoharie County, New York State Police said. Authorities had been searching for Ryan since his father, Robert Ryan, was found dead inside his burning Greenville home Thursday evening. Police said the fire was deliberately set.
Police did not say how Ryan was found or provide details about his arrest. They said more information would be released later.
NEW YORK STATE POLICE LAUNCH MANHUNT AFTER KILLING, HOUSE FIRE FOR 'ARMED AND DANGEROUS' SUSPECT
Thomas David Ryan, 32, was taken into custody in the Gilboa area of Schoharie County, New York State Police said. (New York State Police)
The case began around 7:30 p.m. Thursday, when state troopers were called to a house fire on Greenville Turnpike in Orange County.
After firefighters put out the blaze, a man was found dead inside the home. Police later identified him as Robert Ryan, 70.
Investigators determined the fire had been set intentionally and began treating Robert Ryan’s death as a homicide. Police soon began searching for his son.
Firefighters battled a blaze at this home on Greenville Turnpike in Greenville, N.Y. on Thursday, Aug. 6, 2026. (FOX5 New York)
Ryan did not live with his father and had no other known ties to the Greenville area at the time, according to State Police.
'AMERICA'S MOST WANTED' FUGITIVE CAPTURED ON SAILBOAT OFF NJ COAST AFTER 20 YEARS ON THE RUN

Investigators believed Ryan left in his father’s gray 2016 Toyota Prius. As the search widened, police repeatedly described him as "armed and dangerous" and urged anyone who spotted him to call 911 rather than approach him.

Police combed through surveillance video from homes and businesses, trying to trace Ryan’s movements after the killing. Residents in Greenville and nearby communities were asked to check footage recorded from about 6 p.m. Thursday through the overnight hours.
Police have not disclosed a possible motive or what charges Thomas Ryan faces. (New York State Police)

Police said Ryan had stayed at shelters across New York and was known to frequent the Plattsburgh area, more than 200 miles north of Greenville. Investigators checked places where he had previously stayed and worked with rail operators because Ryan was known to travel by train.

The investigation eventually involved the FBI, NYPD, the Orange County Sheriff’s Office and police departments in Middletown and Port Jervis, along with several State Police investigative units and other state and county agencies.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Police have not disclosed a possible motive, how Robert Ryan died or what charges Thomas Ryan faces.

title: NORAD fighter jets intercept 2 aircraft near Trump’s golf club, 3rd plane delays his NJ departure
summary: NORAD intercepted two general aviation aircraft over Bedminster after they entered restricted airspace near President Donald Trump’s New Jersey golf club.
story: An F-16 fighter jet was caught on camera closing in on a small airplane near Jefferson Township, New Jersey, outside Trump's Bedminster golf club, where temporary flight restrictions were in place. (Credit: X / Joe Afflerbach)

Officials said at least three general aviation aircraft violated temporary flight restrictions near Bedminster, New Jersey, on Sunday as President Donald Trump spent the weekend at his golf club, where the four-day LIV Golf New York tournament was being held.

The North American Aerospace Defense Command (NORAD) said its F-16 fighter jets intercepted two general aviation aircraft before confirming that a third aircraft also triggered an alert as Trump was preparing to depart the area.

The third incident appeared to delay Trump’s departure by about 13 minutes. During that time, emergency SUVs, law enforcement officers and U.S. Secret Service agents were seen moving into position near the runway where Trump was scheduled to depart around 5 p.m. E.T.

Officials said the first two general aviation aircraft were safely escorted out of the restricted area by NORAD aircraft. The third aircraft "reestablished communications and became compliant before NORAD intervention was required."
PRESIDENT TRUMP RECEIVES BIG CHEERS FROM SPECTATORS DURING LIV GOLF EVENT AT HIS NEW JERSEY CLUB
FILE - A U.S. Air Force F-16 Fighting Falcon aircraft flies in the U.S. Central Command area of responsibility Aug. 5, 2026. (U.S. Air Force photo by Senior Airman Adriana Jordan-Alcaniz)

Video captured one of the first two interceptions, showing the dramatic moment an F-16 fighter jet closed in on what appeared to be a small Cessna aircraft near Jefferson Township, outside Bedminster.
Ahead of Trump landing in New Jersey, NORAD previously said that it would enforce multiple FAA-established temporary flight restrictions over the region this weekend.

Pilots and the public were also told that U.S. Army ground-based defense assets may be present in the area, operating under the Continental U.S. NORAD Region as part of the command’s routine, layered defense.

"These systems are operating under NORAD authorities, constitute a routine component of the command’s layered defense posture and work in tandem with the command’s airborne assets to monitor and protect the airspace," information published by the Defense Visual Information Distribution Service said.
FILE - President Donald Trump visited the Trump National Golf Club Bedminster in Bedminster, N.J., on Aug. 7, 2026. (AFP via Getty Images)
TRUMP DRAWS MUCH DIFFERENT REACTION AT NBA FINALS THAN HE DID AT CFP NATIONAL TITLE GAME

Officials used the incident to remind general aviation pilots to check Notices to Airmen (NOTAMs) before every flight for the latest information on airspace restrictions and other flight procedures, as required by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA).
"Check NOTAMs before EVERY flight!" 1st AF/AFNORTH said in a post on X.

If a pilot becomes intercepted by NORAD aircraft, the pilot should immediately adjust their radio frequency to 121.5 or 243.0, according to information published by the Defense Visual Information Distribution Service.
They should then "turn around to reverse course until receiving additional instructions on one of those frequencies."
FILE - The Trump National Golf Club in Bedminster, New Jersey, hosted the LIV Golf New York event. (Photo by Andrew Mordzynski/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Temporary flight restrictions are often issued to limit aircraft operations in designated areas for presidential movements, major sporting events, national security concerns and other special events.
NORAD often employs a network of radars, satellites, fighter aircraft and other capabilities to identify and respond to potential threats in the North American airspace.

title: Florida man accused of killing nurse mom who helped him despite repeated arrests for threatening her: sheriff
summary: Gibson Nash allegedly beat and strangled his mother, a nurse who had bonded him out of jail and moved to Florida to get him mental health help.
story: Internet searches from conman Brian Walshe and voicemails from his mother, Diana, take center stage in new Fox Nation special on the Ana Walshe murder case.
A Florida man allegedly killed his mother, who had recently bonded him out of jail and had moved to the state to get him mental health help.
Gibson Nash, 21, was charged with first-degree murder after a series of perplexing events eventually led police to his mother’s bloodied body.
Deputies with the Polk County Sheriff’s Office found Margaret Chu Dufour, a 56-year-old nurse, on the floor of her home in Polk County, Florida. It wasn’t their first encounter with her.
About a month before, deputies responded to a "disturbance" at the home involving her moving company.
KENTUCKY MAN ACCUSED OF KIDNAPPING, KILLING WOMAN AND KEEPING HER BODY UNDER TRAILER BEFORE DISPOSAL
Gibson Nash has been charged with first-degree murder of his mother, Margaret Chu Dufour, after allegedly beating and strangling her to death in July. (Polk County Sheriff’s Office)
The "movers tried to upcharge her and charge her more money," Polk County Sheriff Grady Judd said in a news conference on Aug. 5.
After movers left, his deputies helped her finish moving items into her new home "without fanfare," Judd said.
"That’s the kind of customer service our deputies do."
So deputies with the same department were horrified to find her dead on the floor a month later. It was the culmination of a series of puzzling events on the morning of July 21, Judd said.
Just before 7 a.m., her son was involved in multiple traffic crashes while driving her vehicle, a blue BMW SUV, Judd said.

After fleeing the first crash, Nash allegedly hit a slew of other vehicles with the SUV, Judd said. The rampage caused more property damage, additional crashes between other vehicles and ultimately injuries to three people who were treated at a hospital.
Deputies then found Nash unconscious behind the wheel of the SUV covered in blood. That confused deputies, Judd said.
"It was a significant crash, but it was like, ‘Why is he unconscious?’" Judd said.
Deputies tried to sort it out at the scene.
"He's got blood on his hands, and the paramedic thinks this is not a bloody kind of crash. Where did the blood come from?"
DATING-APP CHARMER ACCUSED OF MURDER AFTER HISTORY OF DOMESTIC ARRESTS INVOLVING WOMEN HE MET ONLINE
Margaret Chu Dufour, a 56-year-old nurse, was found beaten and strangled inside her Polk County home, authorities said. (Polk County Sheriff’s Office)
Nash was taken to a local hospital with an unknown identity. He was sedated and intubated.
Meanwhile, deputies went to Dufour’s house because it was shown on the vehicle’s registration. She didn’t answer their knock at the door.
They learned that she wasn’t supposed to be at work that day. They saw a broken glass plate near her patio door and a shovel near the side of the house.
Because of the "suspicious circumstances," they entered the house with a key they found on the front porch, according to the Polk County Sheriff’s Office.
Deputies then found Dufour "stomped into a bloody puddle in the middle of the floor," Judd said.
The medical examiner said she died from "blunt force injury from a beating, and from being strangled to death," Judd said.
"It’s one of the most, personally, violent murders we've seen in a very long time," said the sheriff, who’s been in law enforcement 54 years.

In April, Nash had been arrested twice for allegedly threatening to kill his mother. They both lived in Knoxville, Tennessee, at the time. The first time, Dufour had called 911 after locking the door behind her after entering a smoke shop, leaving him in her vehicle just outside.

She told the 911 operator that her son had "attacked" her the night before and "assaulted" her that morning, Judd said. The only way she could get him to calm down was agreeing to take him to the smoke shop, she said on the call.

Shortly after, Nash was arrested for allegedly threatening to kill her with a knife. Later that month, Nash pulled a knife and threatened to kill her again, this time "over not being able to play on the Xbox," Judd said.
DISPATCHER HEARD 'LOUD BANG' BEFORE TIKTOK INFLUENCER WHO OUTED ALLEGED PEDOPHILE HUSBAND FOUND DEAD: AUDIO
Margaret Chu Dufour moved into a new home in Eagle Lake, Fla., about a month before she was killed. (Polk County Sheriff’s Office)
Soon after, Dufour moved to Florida. But she returned to Tennessee to bond her son out of jail, Judd said.
Her move south was an attempt to get Nash more mental health treatment, Judd said. Family members told investigators that he’s "bipolar, schizophrenic and maybe autistic."

title: Miss North Carolina USA pageant producers fire back after winner says she lost title over faith
summary: Brittany Boltinhouse claims her conservative Christian beliefs cost her the Miss North Carolina USA crown, but organizers cite her repeated N-word use.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

The stripping of a Miss North Carolina USA winner's crown was due to "the totality of the circumstances" of her past objectionable speech and not her conservative politics or Christian beliefs, according to organizers.

"A Blaize Productions’ decision was not based on Brittany Boltinhouse’s political views, religious beliefs, or protected personal viewpoints," according to a statement released by the organization that holds the North Carolina state license for the Miss USA pageant.
"Our organization includes people from various backgrounds, political views, personal beliefs and values. We welcome and celebrate that."
FORMER MISS NORTH CAROLINA USA SAYS CONSERVATIVE CHRISTIAN VALUES PLAYED ROLE IN LOSING CROWN

"I believe and think I was stripped from my title because of my political stance and my belief system as a conservative Christian woman," Brittany Boltinhouse, a member of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, told the Carolina Journal in an interview Friday. (Instagram/espino.sosa)

Brittany Boltinhouse, 27, won the Miss North Carolina USA pageant in June but only held the crown for weeks after her past online posts were scrutinized. She was stripped of her crown this week and said her views and past public statements were the reason.

"I believe and think I was stripped from my title because of my political stance and my belief system as a conservative Christian woman," Boltinhouse, a member of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, told the Carolina Journal in an interview Friday.
"I am proud of my faith. I am proud of my standards. I am a proud conservative woman, but a Christian woman. I'm a God-fearing woman."
"I will never let my guard down for my faith, and also I love this country."
MISS NORTH CAROLINA USA LOSES CROWN AFTER ORGANIZER CONDEMNS 'RACISM, HOMOPHOBIA, TRANSPHOBIA'

story: Surveillance video shows the moments before Venezuelan national Carlos Suarez-Contreras allegedly backed his SUV into Deborah Murphy and killed her in the parking lot of a Publix store in Panama City, Florida. (Florida Highway Patrol)
Two Florida men have been charged with aggravated battery after allegedly taking up arms — one with a machete and one with a hatchet — in a Publix parking lot.
The Aug. 4 "physical altercation" between Everette Krichbaum, 52, and James Gay, 35, was over a love interest, according to a police report.
Detectives reported Gay was the "primary aggressor" in the incident in Panama City.
Everette Krichbaum, left, and James Gay have been charged with aggravated battery. (Bay County Sheriff's Office)
VIDEO SHOWS MOMENTS BEFORE ARMY VETERAN WAS FATALLY SHOT IN WALMART PARKING LOT DISPUTE

Gay then allegedly returned to his vehicle and came back with a machete in its sheath. He hit Krichbaum in the face with it, the document shows.

‘VIBRANT’ FLORIDA GRANDMA ALLEGEDLY KILLED BY ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT OUTSIDE PUBLIX, FAMILY FIGHTS FOR JUSTICE
James Gay and Stephanie Marshall have been dating since June, Marshall told Fox News Digital on Aug. 5, 2026. (Courtesy of Stephanie Marshall)

MYRTLE BEACH MAN WITH LENGTHY ARREST RECORD CHARGED WITH STABBING TWO PEOPLE IN POPULAR BEACH DESTINATION

Shoppers use the crosswalk in front of a Publix supermarket in Alachua, Fla., on July 20, 2026. (Natasha Holt for Fox News Digital)
