title: Tan France Responds to Karamo Brown Saying ‘Queer Eye’ Was a ‘Nightmare’
summary: Tan France shared his reaction to fellow “Queer Eye” castmate Karamo Brown’s assertion there was a toxic culture on the set of the show before its conclusion after 10 seasons earlier this year.
story: Tan France shared his reaction to fellow “Queer Eye” castmate Karamo Brown’s assertion that there was a toxic culture on the set of the show before its conclusion after 10 seasons earlier this year.

In a People magazine cover story in June titled “Surviving My Reality TV Nightmare,” Brown said he clashed with some of his costars, describing bullying from executives and production members and opened up about relapsing in 2018 during the third season of the show.
France, 43, spoke with Jenna Bush Hager and Sheinelle Jones on TODAY Aug. 6 about Brown’s comments.

“First of all, I’m sad that was the experience that he felt like it was a nightmare, as I said it was a dream for me,” France said. “I couldn’t believe it. And so for me, I look back thinking, gosh, we did what I think was incredible work and had a phenomenal experience.
“I’m so proud of what we did, and all I want is for the audience to remember that. I want them to know that it was so real for me on that show. Every experience that I had was special,” he added.
The Netflix show released its 10th and final season in January. The show’s producers disputed Brown’s claims about the environment on set.

“We strongly disagree with any characterization that concerns raised during the production of ‘Queer Eye’ were ignored, dismissed or allowed to continue unchecked,” the show’s production company, ITV America and Scout Productions, told People at the time.
Brown was set to attend a Jan. 20 interview on TODAY with France and castmates Antoni Porowski, Jonathan Van Ness and Jeremiah Brent to promote the show, but he canceled last-minute.
He explained his absence in a June 23 appearance on TODAY with Jenna & Sheinelle.

“One of the things that I’ve been teaching people right now is that two things can be true at once,” he said. “‘Queer Eye’ was one of the most amazing shows — the impact that it had culturally for 10 years and what we were able to do. One of the things I’ll say about my cast, no matter what we were going through, we always made sure that the hero was No. 1, that the person we were helping, the crew worked so hard.

“But on the flip side, you can also have a bad experience,” he continued. “And you can also feel as if you’re not being protected and things are not going well. So while I loved what we did, it didn’t mean that I loved what was happening to me.”
During the group interview without Brown on TODAY in January, one of his costars remarked on his absence.
“I think (we’re) definitely a little surprised, but at the same time, like, look, we’re so sorry that he’s not here,” Porowski said.
France made it clear in his Aug. 6 appearance on TODAY that he enjoyed his time on the show, which followed a “Fab Five” team of gay professionals giving lifestyle makeovers to guests.

“Now I look back thinking, gosh, we won loads of Emmys, we were nominated for an Emmy again this season, that’s wild after all those years to still feel so positively about your work,” he said. “If they wanted to do another 10 seasons, I’m like yeah, it was the greatest gift of my life.”

The British-born fashion designer also said he’s grateful to have seen so much of the U.S. thanks to his time on “Queer Eye.” He’s currently moving from Salt Lake City to New York City with his husband and two children.

“I am the luckiest man in the world,” he said. “I got to do, in my opinion, the best job in the world with some of the greatest people that you could ever meet. I got to see America through a lens that no one else really gets to.”

title: Iran sets steep demands to reopen Hormuz despite hopes Oman deal could break impasse
summary: Tehran has vowed not to reopen the shipping lane “until America corrects its behavior,” despite a looming agreement with Oman.
story: There are no ongoing negotiations between Tehran and Washington, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Sunday, after Tehran set out a steep series of demands for the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz.
“The intermediaries are still making efforts to find ways to resume negotiations,” Araghchi said.

He tempered optimism stirred by Iran’s separate discussions with Oman over the future management of the waterway, saying that “changes to maritime routes in the Strait of Hormuz are a technical and legal matter and do not mean that the Strait of Hormuz has been reopened.”

Araghchi’s statement came a day after top Iranian security official Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr laid out the country’s conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, saying it would not do so “until America corrects its behavior.”

The statement from Iran’s Supreme National Security Council secretary, as carried by Iranian state media, stated that the U.S. must withdraw its naval blockade, pay Iran damages for the war, unfreeze Iranian assets, lift sanctions on Tehran and permanently end the conflict against Iran and its regional allies.
Even though the demands are steep, analysts say they are still largely within the framework of the initial deal the two sides reached in June.

“The Supreme National Security Council of Iran, which is really a consensus body, they have come to a realization that for them the best route is returning back to the MOU,” Mehran Haghirian, director of research and programs at the Bourse & Bazaar Foundation London-based think tank, said in a phone interview.
“They want to make sure that they get some of those things up-front, or at least there is a process for them before there is any movement on Hormuz.”
The U.S. has yet to respond publicly to the list of conditions. Top officials have previously ruled out making any immediate payments to Iran during past efforts to seal a deal to end the war.

The country’s enriched uranium stockpile has also been a sticking point for Washington, which insists Iran must abandon its nuclear ambitions. The stalled negotiations have left the Strait of Hormuz largely impassable for months, save for brief periods of operation. Thousands of sailors remain stranded in the region, unable to return home or keep the world’s supply of oil flowing.

“What we’re really working through now is how you can actually set up a traffic scheme so that the ships that pass can pass through safely,” Vice President JD Vance told Fox News on Saturday. That scheme, Vance said, would include demining efforts and also assurances from Tehran that it would not fire on transiting vessels.

On Saturday, Oman condemned attacks on the vessels that were attempting to pass through the Strait of Hormuz, saying in a statement that such attacks could affect its negotiations with Iran over the waterway’s management. The UAE and Kuwait on Saturday also condemned an Iranian missile attack on an Abu Dhabi National Oil Co. tanker.
Oman nonetheless said its discussions with Iran were “proceeding in a positive and constructive atmosphere.”

Iran and Oman, neighbors across the Strait of Hormuz, have been negotiating an agreement on how to manage traffic through the waterway, including considerations of a toll fee. The discussions have also been viewed optimistically, raising hopes that they could finally lead to reopening the strait.
But Iranian officials have dismissed any such possibility. Iran’s discussions with Oman do “not mean the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz,” Araghchi said Saturday.

Even though the Iranian officials say the discussions don’t mean an immediate reopening of Hormuz, Haghirian said the discussions would lay critical groundwork for if and when Iran reaches an agreement with the U.S. over Hormuz.

Iranian state media on Sunday reported that President Masoud Pezeshkian had met with the country’s absent Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, discussing “the war and the future ahead.” No evidence was provided that the meeting took place.

Pezeshkian earlier this week said that it had been “very difficult” to contact the 56-year-old leader, who has not been seen publicly since he was badly injured in the U.S. strikes that killed his father.
Meanwhile, the Iran-allied Houthi rebels in Yemen again attacked Saudi Arabia on Sunday, with Yemen’s news agency saying the forces targeted the Mocha port along the Red Sea.

The Houthis have launched several attacks on Saudi Arabia in recent days, also hitting a Saudi Aramco oil refinery in the port city of Jizan with a drone. It said Sunday that the attack on the refinery was in response to Saudi drones’ incursions into the Saada and Hajjah airspaces of Yemen.
The Saudi Energy Ministry said Sunday on X that the fire that broke out at the refinery had been extinguished and nobody was injured.

The world’s top oil exporter, Aramco, is seeking to reroute some of its exports to the Red Sea instead of the Persian Gulf in an effort to circumvent the shuttered Strait of Hormuz. Riyadh on Saturday condemned the attacks by the Houthis, who it said had attacked the kingdom since July 13 and shipping vessels since July 22.

title: Senate passes sanctions bill on Russia and Iran named for late Sen. Lindsey Graham
summary: WASHINGTON — The Senate voted overwhelmingly to pass legislation to impose sanctions against Russia and Iran after months of fits and starts, with the death of Republican Sen.
story: WASHINGTON — The Senate voted overwhelmingly to pass legislation to impose sanctions against Russia and Iran after months of fits and starts, with the death of Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham providing the final push.

The 61-page legislation, renamed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, in honor of the bill’s biggest proponent, is designed to punish major buyers of Russian oil and gas. It also features additional sanctions on Russian leaders, family members and oligarchs.
And it allows for targeted tariffs on products from countries that buy most Russian oil and gas, limiting them to the five biggest importers.
The vote was 86-11.
Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said the bill would help protect Ukraine against Russian aggression.

“Ukraine is now the largest conflict, literally, since World War II in Europe,” Thune said in a recent floor speech. “And the Ukrainian people have been resilient, worked really, really hard to try and bring this war to an end. But as long as Putin has Russian oil and gas money, he’s able to continue this war. And what this sanctions bill would do would basically cut that off.”
After a last-minute demand from President Donald Trump, it also extends sanction authority designed to limit funding toward Iran’s weapons and energy sectors.
The bill has been criticized by a group of Democrats and Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., with the Democrats arguing that it would give Trump too much tariff authority.
It now goes to the Republican-controlled House, where it faces an uncertain future.

The Senate deal was announced Tuesday morning by Sen. Darline Graham, R-S.C., the late senator’s sister and appointed successor, as well as Sens. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn.; Katie Britt, R-Ala.; Jeanne Shaheen, D-N.H.; Roger Wicker, R-Miss.; and Jim Risch, R-Idaho.
The senators struck the deal July 28, less than two weeks after Graham’s unexpected death, saying there was “no greater way to honor” the South Carolinian’s legacy.

“We are proud to announce an agreement on legislation to stop purchasers of Russian oil and gas from fueling Putin’s war machine and to continue restricting the Iranian regime’s ability to support terrorism and build its nuclear program,” the senators said in a joint statement.
Senate passage was all but guaranteed after the chamber voted 86-12 to advance the bill procedurally last month, shortly after reaching the deal.

title: How Spain’s migration surge tested E.U. border policy
summary: An unprecedented surge of migrants into Spanish territory of Ceuta in North Africa marked the first  reignited the European Union’s debate over immigration.
story: Tens of thousands of migrants crossed from Morocco into Ceuta, an autonomous Spanish territory in North Africa, between July 30 and 31. The unexpected crisis overwhelmed local authorities and infrastructure, marking a first test of the European Union’s (E.U.) new Pact on Migration and Asylum. The scale and speed of the crossing exposed a real flash point in Europe’s migration system, but how fast authorities regained control has become its own point of contention—over whether the E.U. system is failing or working as designed.

The surge drew criticism from Washington and European capitals. The State Department claimed that the Spanish government had led efforts “to enable and facilitate mass illegal migration into Europe.” Denmark and Italy led a similar critique at the E.U. level, sending a letter—co-signed by 22 member states—that called for coordinated E.U. border measures and accused Spain of enacting policies that were a “pull factor” for undocumented migrants. Far-right parties across Europe have seized on the crisis to attack Spain and Europe’s migration policy.

Charles A. Kupchan, an expert on European affairs at CFR, explained that the surge came as a shock because migration to the E.U. is generally “more of a trickle than a deluge” in terms of the number of arrivals. “This rush, this mass of humanity, all coming in the span of forty-eight hours is quite unusual, and it’s because of the size, scope, and speed that it caused such a stir,” he said.
While most migrants have since returned to Morocco, the incident has renewed the debate over European border and migration policy — long a thorny political issue.
What happened in Ceuta?

Approximately 72,000 migrants crossed into Ceuta from Moroccan territory in just a few days, according to Spain’s interior minister. (Some reports put this figure at between 50,000 and 60,000.) Most migrants reached Ceuta by sea, either by swimming or using makeshift flotation devices. More than 80 people died on both sides of the border, with many drowning or getting killed in stampedes.

title: Israel rejects Trump’s 15-point plan for Gaza, Netanyahu says
summary: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ⁠said Israeli forces wouldn’t withdraw from the war-torn enclave until Hamas fully disarms
story: Israel will not accept the 15-point plan for Gaza set out by President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Sunday.

“I want to clarify this: Israel rejects the 15-point document. I have heard people saying, ‘You didn’t say that.’ So here I am saying it again,” he told a Cabinet meeting, referring to the peace plan set out by Trump last year. “The IDF will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is disarmed,” he added.
Trump last month touted a breakthrough in his Gaza peace plan, saying that Hamas has agreed to lay down arms.

The peace plan called for a phased withdrawal of Israel’s troops from Gaza alongside the disarmament of Hamas, but Netanyahu said Israeli forces are not going anywhere until Hamas completely disarms first.
“When I say Hamas must be disarmed, I mean heavy weapons, lighter weapons, all weapons. We are talking about genuine disarmament, not a fictitious one,” Netanyahu said Sunday.

Hamas had last month said that it would disarm, but only after Israel withdraws completely and stops all hostilities. The group also said that laying down its heavy weapons would come later in the process, conditional on the establishment of a Palestinian state.

Netanyahu, meanwhile, reaffirmed that “as long as I am prime minister, there will be no Palestinian state.” The leader is currently facing a domestic political battle for survival ahead of elections set for October, with the status of the Gaza and Iran conflicts likely to prove pivotal.

The explicit rejection of the peace plan, frequently touted by Trump as a key foreign policy achievement, also comes after months of growing tensions between the White House and Israel’s leadership over Iran. The White House did not immediately comment on the remarks.

Netanyahu said of Washington: “We are currently discussing this issue with the Americans. They have ideas; some of them are acceptable to us and some are not, and we know how to stand firm on these matters.”

The Israeli leader may consider it worthwhile to “enter a new confrontation with President Trump,” said Ronni Shaked, a research fellow at the Harry S. Truman Institute at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, as his own popularity wanes ahead of October’s election.

“After three years, he is without any victory, and he just wants to show now to the people of Israel, before the election, that look at me, I have victory, and the victory is that we are going to disarm Hamas,” Shaked said in a phone interview, referring to the tactic as an “illusion.”

Responding to Netanyahu’s statement Sunday, senior Hamas official Basim Naeem said that the group expects the mediators and the U.S. to “exert pressure” on Netanyahu and his government to abide by the road map and “prevent him from obstructing the process for domestic political and electoral considerations.”

A further Hamas statement reaffirmed its commitment to the agreed-upon road map, reiterating the group’s “seriousness in engaging responsibly in implementing the fifteen points agreed upon and establishing a clear timetable for their implementation.”

Mohammad Dahlan, a member of the Palestinian Legislative Council, said Netanyahu’s announcement “represents a challenge, contempt, and deception of the American administration and President Trump’s team,” adding that Washington “now realizes that Netanyahu is an obstacle to achieving security and stability.”

Netanyahu’s far-right finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, welcomed his announcement after seeking to pressure the leader into a more hard-line stance. “I congratulate the Prime Minister for responding to our demand and clarifying unequivocally,” he said on X.

Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty meanwhile “emphasized the necessity for all parties to fulfill their commitments and refrain from taking any actions that could hinder the implementation process or undermine the progress achieved,” his office said in a statement.
Add NBC News to Google
Add NBC News to Google

Despite agreeing to halt attacks last October, Israel has continued its deadly strikes on the enclave. On Saturday, recovery operations concluded at the Karam Building in Gaza after 19 bodies were found under the rubble, according to the Gaza civil defense. Israel and Hamas both regularly accuse the other of breaching the ceasefire.

Over 73,000 people have been killed in Gaza since Oct. 7, 2023, according to the enclave’s health officials, including over 1,200 people since the ceasefire began in October. Israel said it launched its war in Gaza in response to the Hamas-led attack in which around 1,200 people were killed and 251 others taken hostage.

title: Student kills multiple people at Thai school after fatally shooting grandparents
summary: At least one teacher was killed and four other people injured by a student who opened fire at a school in Thailand on Friday before killing himself, authorities said.
story: BANGKOK — A gunman shot and killed his grandparents before killing five people and himself at a school outside Bangkok on Friday, Thailand’s prime minister said, in the Southeast Asian nation’s worst mass killing since 2022.

Anutin Charnvirakul told a news conference that five teachers were shot dead and at least 30 people were injured in the shooting at Debsirin Nonthaburi School in the Bang Kruai district of Nonthaburi province, north of Bangkok. The shooter took his own life, he added.

The perpetrator was identified as a student and police said that he had fired at least 26 rounds and that 34 other rounds of ammunition were found at the scene. They said they had recovered a 9 mm handgun believed to belong to his grandfather.
At least two people were in critical condition, police said.
One 18-year-old student told Reuters that at first he thought he was hearing firecrackers.
“Then it started getting more frequent, like ‘bang, bang, bang’ and then it went quiet at one point,” he said. “And the shooting started again.”
In a statement, the school said the shooting had “shaken the hearts” of students, parents, teachers and others.
The government said Anutin had directed relevant agencies to provide immediate and comprehensive support to all those affected.

“We rushed to care for the injured and I have dispatched the relevant personnel to handle the situation at the site,” Anutin told reporters. “This is very terrible, it is something that should not have happened.”
It is the second school shooting in Thailand this year.
One teacher was killed and a student was injured in February at a school in the southern district of Hat Yai.
In recent years, there has been a series of deadly shootings at schools and other locations in Thailand, where gun ownership is common.
Last year, six people were killed when a man opened fire at a Bangkok market before taking his own life.
In 2023, a 14-year-old killed two people and injured five others in a shooting at a luxury mall in Bangkok.

The previous year, a former police officer killed 36 people during a three-hour shooting and stabbing spree in the country’s northeast. Among his victims were 22 children he stabbed at a day care center.
A Thai soldier also killed 29 people in a shooting rampage in the northeastern city of Nakhon Ratchasima in 2020.

After the 2023 mall shooting, Anutin, who was interior minister at the time, enacted a one-year ban on the issue of new personal gun licenses and suspended public carry permits, among other gun control measures. The suspension of public carry permits was extended earlier this year.
“This is the reason why the government doesn’t allow arm carrying and extension of gun licenses,” Anutin said Friday. “This is the reason why.”

Anutin also vowed to introduce a new firearms control law in Southeast Asia’s largest gun-owning nation, according to Reuters. “The new law will only allow government officials on duty to carry guns,” the agency reported him saying.

As of 2017, Thai civilians were estimated to possess about 10.3 million firearms, or about 15 per 100 residents, according to the Small Arms Survey, a Swiss group that favors gun control. That compared with more than 393 million firearms in civilian possession in the United States, or 120.5 per 100 residents.
Nat Sumon reported from Bangkok, and Jennifer Jett from Hong Kong.

title: Trump administration revokes Brazilian ambassador’s visa in diplomatic dispute
summary: The Trump administration revoked the visa of Brazil’s U.S. ambassador Tuesday — the latest jab in a monthslong diplomatic spat between the two countries.
story: The Trump administration revoked the visa of Brazil’s U.S. ambassador Tuesday — the latest jab in a monthslong diplomatic spat between the two countries.

The U.S. action was taken in retaliation for Brazil’s withholding formal approval for the Trump administration’s pick for U.S. ambassador to Brazil, Florida House Speaker Daniel Perez, a senior State Department official told reporters Tuesday.
The official, who spoke on behalf of the State Department on condition of anonymity, said Brazil has indicated the approval is likely to be delayed until after its election in October.
The Brazilian government said it repudiates the visa revocation of their ambassador, calling both justifications from the U.S. “false,” and noted that the U.S. request remains under review.

“It should be recalled that individual sanctions against Brazilian officials remain in force, notably the cancellation of U.S. visas based on the unfounded allegation that former President Bolsonaro is being subjected to political persecution,” the office of the president of Brazil said in a statement. “Those affected include Supreme Court justices and senior members of the Executive Branch.”
Jair Bolsonaro was the president of Brazil before President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.

The Brazilian president’s office said the decision “is not an isolated incident,” and “forms part of a deliberate escalation of hostile measures against Brazil, driven by ideological motives that are incompatible with a bilateral partnership that has always been guided by mutual respect.”

The tit-for-tat has been ongoing since at least March, when Brazil denied visas to a U.S. delegation traveling to a critical minerals forum, the U.S. official said. In July, Brazil also denied visas to two U.S. officials, accusing them of plotting to meddle in Brazil’s electoral process.
“This week we had to deny visas to two young folks they were sending to Brazil to meddle in Brazil’s elections,” Lula said at an event last Wednesday.

The senior State Department official denied the accusations and said the assistant secretary for democracy, human rights and labor, Riley M. Barnes, and one of his deputies, Samuel Samson, “were making a routine trip” and were “denied the ability to do routine, common work between the two countries.”

“We’ve taken reciprocal action with respect to the Brazilian diplomat here to make the point that it can’t always be one-sided,” the senior State Department official said. “If there’s going to be limitations on one side’s diplomats, they will be reciprocated.”

The official clarified that Brazilian Ambassador Maria Luiza Ribeiro Viotti will not be expelled from the U.S. but warned that additional diplomatic options remain on the table if the Brazilian government continues to delay or refuse to approve the U.S. ambassador nominee. If Viotti leaves the country, she would need to reapply for a visa, the official said, adding that the Brazilian ambassador’s visa will be reinstated if Brazil approves Perez.

“We communicated continually with the Brazilian government for weeks and have given the Brazilian government every opportunity to do the right thing, yet they have continually delayed and obfuscated,” the official said. “President Trump has the right to determine who represents the American people and interests around the world.”

“President Trump is assembling an America First diplomatic A-team across his administration, subject to the advice and consent of the Senate. We reject any effort by foreign countries to interfere in our domestic processes,” the official added.
